`AGENTS.md`:

```md
# Tag Kit for Steam

An MV3 extension for Chromium-based browsers and Firefox, plus a Tampermonkey/Violentmonkey
userscript, built from one TypeScript core, that tag Steam store items: AI Generated Content Disclosure, anti-cheat, 3rd-party DRM, 3rd-Party Account, 3rd-party EULA and PvP.

## Working knowledge (docs/)

- Plans: `docs/plans/<slug>.md`, one per piece of work, with a status header (draft, active, done, dropped).
- Research: `docs/research/<topic>.md` summary plus `docs/research/<topic>/rqN-<slug>.md` notes.
- Journal: `docs/journal/YYYY-MM-DD.md`, append-only, one line per unit of work.
- Drafts: `docs/drafts/` holds prose in progress; `*.review.md` sidecars are git-excluded.
- Decisions: `docs/adr/`, MADR format in `.mdx`, one ADR per choice with real alternatives.
- Design: `docs/design/` holds the UI tokens and component specs; `assets/icons/` the icons.
- `docs/TASKS.md` is personal and untracked; never commit it.

## Project rules

These are hard rules. A change that breaks one needs an ADR first.

1. **Privacy.** App IDs leave the browser only for Valve hosts the user is already on:
   `api.steampowered.com` (GetItems) and `store.steampowered.com` (app pages). Every such request
   uses `credentials: "omit"`. No analytics, no third-party hosts, no seed lists, no server of our
   own.
2. **No remote code.** No `eval`, `new Function`, remote scripts or remote selector logic. Bundles
   are not minified.
3. **Permissions.** `storage` plus content-script matches on `https://store.steampowered.com/*`.
   No `host_permissions` and no background script unless an ADR says otherwise.
4. **Semantics.** Three verdict states: disclosed, not disclosed, unknown. Unknown is never stored
   or shown as not disclosed. An item without `extra_details` is unknown; an item with
   `extra_details` and no key for a kind is not reported. Neither state renders as "none", "DRM-free"
   or "no anti-cheat". A tag uses Steam's own words for its kind, and our own copy never says
   "uses AI", "AI-free" or "no AI". The developer's own text is rendered verbatim through
   `textContent`.
5. **Core purity.** `src/core` uses only DOM and web standards and never names `chrome`, `browser`
   or `GM`. Platform code lives in `src/platform/`.
6. **Originality and credit.** No code is copied from other AI-disclosure extensions, and nothing
   from GPL projects such as Augmented Steam. Ideas are credited in the README.
   `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` lists the licenses of bundled dependencies and of third-party artwork in
   the bundle.
7. **One version source.** The `package.json` version feeds both manifests and the userscript
   header. Feature changes never edit it; the release pipeline does.
8. **Repo hygiene.** Repo text is ASCII with normal capitalization and no em dashes (non-English
   catalogs excepted). Branches are `<type>/<slug>`. Commits follow Conventional Commits 1.0.0 with
   the types `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `perf`, `style`, `test`, `docs`, `build`, `ops`, `chore`
   (CI changes are `build`), and carry no trailers.
9. **i18n from day 1.** Every user-visible or logged message (UI copy, errors, warnings, notices,
   ARIA labels, tooltips, manifest and userscript names and descriptions) lives in a message
   catalog under `src/locales/`, keyed and typed. Code and tests read copy from the catalog and
   hold keys, never copy: a test takes its expected text from `t(key, params)` or the catalog
   JSON. `scripts/check_i18n.py` fails on catalog text typed as a string literal under `src/` or
   `tests/`; `tests/locales/` and `tests/fixtures/` are exempt. Allowed literals: identifiers,
   selectors, URLs, storage keys, CSS class names, and detection constants such as Steam's own
   `AI Generated Content Disclosure` heading.
10. **Strict static typing.** No `any`, explicit or implicit. Untrusted input is `unknown` until a
    validation schema turns it into a typed value. No type assertions other than `as const`, no
    non-null assertions, no `@ts-ignore` or `@ts-nocheck`. Branded types for domain IDs,
    discriminated unions with exhaustive checks, `readonly` by default.
11. **SOLID and DRY.** One module, one reason to change. New store surfaces are new placement
    entries and new detection sources are new detector links; the scanner and the chain are not
    edited for them. Every port implementation passes the shared contract tests. Ports stay small.
    Core depends only on ports; the extension content script and the userscript entry are the only
    shipped composition roots (`src/platform/dev/inject.ts` is a dev-only root, never packaged).
    Before writing new code, check whether existing code can be refactored to cover the case.
12. **Library check first.** Before building anything non-trivial, look for a library that does it
    and study it (size, types, maintenance, license, whether we need it at all). Record the outcome
    in the ADR or PR description.
13. **Efficiency.** Performance and memory are requirements:
    - one GetItems request per batch of up to 50 unseen app IDs, none for cached verdicts;
    - after the first pass, scan only added DOM subtrees; batch DOM reads before writes; dim and
      hide are CSS attribute selectors; no polling;
    - `WeakSet`/`WeakMap` keyed by elements, no per-node closures or listeners, a bounded
      in-memory cache, observers disconnected on `pagehide`;
    - bundle size and scan-time budgets are enforced by checks.
14. **mise is the only toolchain manager and task runner.** Local development, Git hooks, CI and
    release pipelines all run `mise run <task>`. Every tool is pinned in `mise.toml`; JavaScript
    libraries loaded from `node_modules` (esbuild, TypeScript, oxlint, valibot, vitest) are
    exact-pinned in `package.json` and the lockfile. Non-trivial logic lives in `scripts/` as `.sh`
    (short glue) or `.py` (anything with logic), called only from mise tasks; lint configuration
    such as the oxlint plugin in `lint/` is not task logic. `package.json` holds dependencies and
    no scripts. The pre-commit hook runs `mise run precommit`; the pre-push hook runs
    `mise run prepush`.
15. **Formatting.** Line width 100 for every file we own: TypeScript, JSON, CSS, HTML, YAML, TOML,
    Python and shell. Markdown and MDX are formatted for structure only; prose is not wrapped.
    `precommit` formats staged files and re-stages them; `prepush` and CI reject unformatted
    files. Captured fixtures, the lockfile and `LICENSE` are excluded.
16. **Secrets.** `STEAM_API_KEY` is read only by development scripts, only from the environment.
    It is never committed, logged, written into fixtures or bundled; a build check fails if its
    value appears in `dist/` or `artifacts/`. Release secrets live in GitHub environments.

## Development browsers

- Gecko testing uses Firefox Nightly only, through a dedicated profile. The regular Firefox
  install is personal: never launch it, install into it, or touch its profiles.
- Chromium (not the regular Chrome release) is the project's Chromium browser and is used only for
  this project; loading the unpacked build there is fine.
- Machine-specific paths (`SAR_GECKO_BIN`, `SAR_GECKO_PROFILE`, `SAR_CHROMIUM_BIN`,
  `SAR_CHROMIUM_PROFILE`) live in the gitignored `mise.local.toml` of the main checkout. Edit it
  there; `.worktreeinclude` copies it into each new worktree, and an older worktree copies it by
  hand.
- The Claude desktop app's built-in browser cannot load extensions; agents use it to inject the
  dev bundle (`dist/dev/inject.js`) for smoke tests on live store pages.

## Workflow

- Trunk-based: every change reaches `main` through a PR from its own `<type>/<slug>` branch,
  squash-merged with the PR title (a Conventional Commit header) as the commit message.
- Sessions spawned for a piece of work run in their own Git worktree and branch, never in the
  shared checkout. They push and open the PR; the main session reviews and merges.
- After a merge: archive the session, remove its worktree and branch, and rebase any open branch
  that the merge left behind onto `main`.
- PR descriptions carry no AI attribution or trailers.
- On GitHub, sessions may push branches, open PRs, add labels and close superseded PRs. They
  change repo settings only after explicit approval. They post no comments, reviews or issues.
- Plans in `docs/plans/` and research in `docs/research/` stay committed in this repo, since ADRs
  link to the research. Code never references either.
- Main tasks: `mise run setup` once per clone, then `fmt`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `test`, `build`,
  `check`, `ci`; `dev`, `run-gecko`, `run-chromium` to try builds; `change-new` for changelog notes.

`PRIVACY.md`:

```md
# Privacy

Tag Kit for Steam collects nothing. It has no analytics, no telemetry, no account, no server of its own and no third-party hosts. It sends no reports anywhere, and nothing is sent to the developer.

## What is stored on your device

- Results per app ID: which tags the store data gives the item, the time it was checked, the developer's AI report text and its language, the name of a named AI service if there is one, and the game's name.
- Your settings: whether badges and the banner are on, the list filter mode (off, dim or hide), the language, and a debug flag.
- Your allow-list of games you chose to ignore (app ID, name and date).
- A small internal record used to back off if Steam is limiting requests.

This lives in the extension's local storage (`storage.local`) or, in the userscript, in your userscript manager's storage. It never leaves your browser, and you can clear it by removing the extension or the userscript. The extension requests only the `storage` permission and runs only on `https://store.steampowered.com/*`.

## What is sent, and where

To find out which tags an item has, the app IDs of the items on the page you are viewing are sent to Valve, and only to Valve:

- `https://api.steampowered.com/IStoreBrowseService/GetItems/v1`: the app IDs on the page, in batches of up to 50, with the page's Steam language to get the developer's text translated.
- `https://store.steampowered.com/app/<id>/?l=english`: a fallback that fetches an app's store page when the API gives no answer, for a few apps per page view.

Every one of these requests is made without cookies (`credentials: "omit"`), so Steam does not receive your login or session from it. Valve sees your IP address and the app IDs, as it does for any store request. These are the same hosts your browser already talks to while you browse the store.

Cached results are reused: a checked app is not requested again until its entry expires.

## What is never read or sent

The extension does not read your Steam account, wishlist contents, library, cookies or browsing history, and does not send app IDs, settings or any other data to any other host.

## Not affiliated with Valve

This is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Valve Corporation.

## Changes

If this policy changes, the change is made in this file and in the project's release notes.

```

`README.md`:

```md
<p align="center">
  <img
    src="assets/icons/mark-purple.svg"
    alt="Tag Kit for Steam logo: a purple Steam badge with a tag at its lower right"
    width="96"

# Tag Kit for Steam

A browser extension for Chromium-based browsers and Firefox, and a userscript (Tampermonkey and Violentmonkey) that tag items on the Steam store with what Valve's own data says about them: AI Generated Content Disclosure, Anti-Cheat (Kernel Level flagged separately), 3rd-party DRM, 3rd-Party Account, 3rd-party EULA and PvP (friend request).

> Status: [releases](https://github.com/jrv97/steam-ai-reporter/releases) are on GitHub. The Firefox link below is a placeholder.

The extension only reads what Steam's store data and developers report there, and sends no reports anywhere.

## Why

Steam Next Fest is, I kid you not, one of my favorite times of the year. I try the demos but never get to play as many as I'd like, and I still browse every corner of the fest and wishlist a bunch of games. Too often a game looks great until I find out it leans heavily on generative AI for its creative work, from gameplay design to art and music. For me personally, that is where I draw the line: creative work done with AI is a hard stop.

I couldn't find an extension that covered every corner of the store and let me preview and review what a developer reported right from the list, without opening the game's page. So I built one. I know this is "querer ponerle puertas al campo" (trying to put doors on an open field), but it's the best I can do, and more importantly, it's fun :)

Once I got that working in place, I thought "why not also flag all the other annoying stuff I keep checking manually like KLAC and 3rd-party accounts?". If you browse the store the same way, I hope you find it useful too :)

## What it does

- Tags these kinds of items: AI Generated Content Disclosure, Kernel Level Anti-Cheat and other Anti-Cheat Software, 3rd-party DRM, 3rd-Party Account, 3rd-party EULA and PvP.
- Adds a badge to capsules and rows (search, wishlist, home, tag and category hubs, sale pages such as Next Fest, developer and publisher pages, the discovery queue, search suggestions) for items that carry one of those tags. Each tag has a short chip (AI, KLAC, Anti-Cheat, DRM, Account, EULA, PvP), and a +N chip stands for the tags that do not fit.
- Opens a card on hover or keyboard focus that lists every tag in Steam's words and ends with a line naming the developer as the source.
- Shows a non-blocking banner on the app page that lists each tag the developer declared and quotes the developer's AI report verbatim.
- Gives each tag its own switch, badge, banner entry and list filter (Show, Dim or Hide). Filters start on Show, and the strongest filter wins when a game carries several tags. The PvP tag starts switched off.
- Lets you ignore a game you consider a false flag, for one tag or for all tags.

Each tag follows Steam's own words:

- AI Generated Content Disclosure: the developer reported generative AI use. The chip reads "AI", and the card and the banner carry Steam's heading "AI Generated Content Disclosure".
- Kernel Level Anti-Cheat: the game's anti-cheat runs at the kernel level. The chip reads "KLAC".
- Anti-Cheat Software: the game uses anti-cheat software.
- 3rd-party DRM: the game uses DRM from a third party.
- 3rd-Party Account: the game needs an account with a third party.
- 3rd-party EULA: the game needs agreement to a third party's EULA.
- PvP: the game has player-versus-player play.

The AI badge does not say a game uses AI, and the absence of a badge does not mean a game is AI-free: the report comes from the developer, and the badge marks what developers chose to report.

### On the store

![Steam search results for "roguelike", where three rows carry an "AI use reported" badge after the game's name](docs/store/screenshots/01-search.jpg)

In search results, rows of games whose developers reported AI use carry the badge after the name.

![A game's store page with a purple banner above the purchase box that reads "AI use reported" and quotes the developer's report; the DLC rows below are badged too](docs/store/screenshots/02-app-banner.jpg)

On a game's page, a banner above the purchase box quotes the developer's report in their own words. The page's DLC rows get badges too. "Ignore this game" stops the badges and the banner for that game in this extension and does not touch Steam's own Ignore button.

![A search row's badge with a panel open below it that quotes the developer's report](docs/store/screenshots/03-hover-card.jpg)

Hovering or tabbing to a badge opens a panel in the style of Steam's game hover, with the developer's own text, any AI service they named and a line for each other tag the game carries.

![Next Fest sale cards where two game images carry a small "AI use reported" badge in their corner](docs/store/screenshots/04-next-fest.jpg)

Sale pages such as Next Fest, tag and category hubs and the home page get a compact badge on the game's image.

### Settings

![The options page: switches for badges and the banner, a Show, Dim and Hide control for lists, a language picker, and a list of games you ignored](docs/store/screenshots/05-options.jpg)

The options page has one section per tag with switches for the tag, its badge and its banner entry, and a Show, Dim and Hide control for lists. Each section can be closed, and the page remembers which ones. It also picks the language (automatic follows the store page) and lists the games you ignored under the scope you ignored them for, each with "Stop ignoring".

![The same search results with the list filter set to Dim, where the three badged rows are faded](docs/store/screenshots/list-dim.jpg)

With the list filter on Dim, badged games fade in lists and come back on hover. Hide removes them from lists. Show, the default, leaves lists as they are.

<img src="docs/store/screenshots/popup.jpg" alt="The toolbar popup with the badge and banner switches, the Show, Dim and Hide control, one game you ignored, and a link to all settings" width="360">

The toolbar popup holds the same per-tag switches and list filters and the games you ignored, with a link to the full options page. The userscript opens the same settings in a dialog from the script manager's menu.

### Known gaps

- In the header's search suggestions on a game's own store page, the suggestion for that same game gets no badge. The banner on the page shows its report.

## Development

Requirements: [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev) and Git. mise installs every other tool at the pinned version (Node, pnpm, Python, uv, dprint, ruff, mypy, shellcheck, shfmt, actionlint, zizmor, changie, gh, web-ext), and pnpm installs the JavaScript libraries (esbuild, TypeScript, oxlint, valibot, vitest) and the test DOM (happy-dom) from the lockfile. On Windows, use Git for Windows; see `mise.local.toml.example` for putting Git Bash ahead of WSL's `bash` when running tasks from PowerShell.

```bash
mise trust
mise run setup
```

`setup` installs the tools and the JavaScript dependencies, writes the pre-commit and pre-push Git hooks, and checks the browser paths. Copy `mise.local.toml.example` to `mise.local.toml` (ignored by Git) and set `SAR_GECKO_BIN` and `SAR_GECKO_PROFILE` (Firefox Nightly and a profile dedicated to this project), plus `SAR_CHROMIUM_BIN` and `SAR_CHROMIUM_PROFILE` (Chromium and its own profile).

Main tasks:

- `mise run fmt`: format every file we own (width 100; Markdown is formatted for structure only).
- `mise run lint`, `mise run typecheck`, `mise run test`: oxlint with type-aware rules, ruff, mypy, shellcheck, actionlint and zizmor; TypeScript 7; vitest with happy-dom.
- `mise run build`: build `dist/chromium`, `dist/gecko`, `dist/userscript` and the dev-only `dist/dev`.
- `mise run check`: text, catalog, version and bundle checks on top of the build.
- `mise run ci`: everything CI runs. The pre-push hook runs `prepush`, which is the same without the reproducibility check and `web-ext lint`.
- `mise run dev`: rebuild on change. In another terminal, `mise run run-gecko` (Firefox Nightly only) or `mise run run-chromium` loads the build with auto-reload.
- `mise run package`: write the Chromium and Gecko zips, the userscript and its `.meta.js`, and the source archive for store reviewers to `artifacts/`, then check them.
- `mise run canary`: before a release, check that live Steam still answers in the shape the detectors expect (four requests). It is not part of `ci`.
- `mise run capture-fixtures`: refresh the public test fixtures from the live store.
- `mise run icons`: render the extension icon PNGs in `assets/icons/` from `mark-purple.svg` with headless Chromium (`SAR_CHROMIUM_BIN`).
- `mise run change-new`: add a changelog fragment. A pull request that changes `src/` needs one, unless it carries the `no-changelog-fragment` label.

### Try a build in your browser

For the quick loop, `mise run run-chromium` or `mise run run-gecko` builds, opens the browser with the dedicated profile from `mise.local.toml` and reloads the extension after each rebuild. Run `mise run dev` in another terminal to rebuild on every change.

To test what a release ships, run `mise run package`. It writes these files to `artifacts/`:

- `steam-ai-reporter-chromium-<version>.zip` and `steam-ai-reporter-gecko-<version>.zip`.
- `steam-ai-reporter.user.js` and `steam-ai-reporter.meta.js`.
- `steam-ai-reporter-source-<version>.zip`, the archive for store reviewers.

`<version>` is the `package.json` version, which holds the last release, so a local package carries that number. Load it like this:

- Chromium: open `chrome://extensions`, turn on Developer mode, choose "Load unpacked" and pick `dist/chromium`. Chromium cannot load the zip.
- Firefox Nightly: open `about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox`, choose "Load Temporary Add-on" and pick the Gecko zip. The browser removes it on restart.
- Userscript: open `artifacts/steam-ai-reporter.user.js` in Tampermonkey or Violentmonkey.

Run `mise run ci` before trusting a package. It adds the reproducibility check and `web-ext lint`.

## Build from source

For store reviewers and anyone who wants to reproduce a release. The build runs on Linux, macOS and Windows; releases are built on Ubuntu 24.04. The source archive in each release (`steam-ai-reporter-source-<version>.zip`) holds everything below needs, including the lockfiles. It leaves out `docs/` apart from `docs/design/tokens.css`, which the build reads.

1. Install mise: `curl https://mise.run | sh` (see [mise's install guide](https://mise.jdx.dev/getting-started.html) for other options).
2. In the source folder, run `mise trust`, then `mise install`. This installs the exact tool versions pinned in `mise.toml` and `mise.lock`.
3. Run `mise run build`. It installs the JavaScript dependencies from `pnpm-lock.yaml` and writes the unminified bundles to `dist/` (`dist/gecko` is the Firefox add-on).

`mise run check-reproducible` builds twice and fails if any output byte differs.

## Releasing

[ADR 0005](docs/adr/0005-release-pipeline.mdx) records the design. Versions are unpadded CalVer: `2026.10.21`, and `2026.10.21.1` for a recut on the same day. The `package.json` version holds the last release, and feature pull requests never edit it.

1. A pull request that changes `src/` adds a changelog fragment with `mise run change-new`.
2. The `release-train` workflow runs at 00:00 UTC or on demand. `gh workflow run release-train.yml -f dry_run=true` reports the version it would cut and opens nothing. A real run opens a batch pull request that bumps the version and writes the changelog, and the pull request merges when the checks pass. With no fragments there is no release.
3. After CI passes on the merged batch commit, the pipeline tags it. `release-nightly` builds once, checks that the build reproduces, and publishes a GitHub prerelease with the five artifacts from `mise run package`. No store is touched. Install the prerelease by hand to test it.
4. To ship, run `gh workflow run release-prod.yml --ref <tag> -f tag=<tag>`. It promotes the prerelease artifacts without a rebuild. The Chrome Web Store and AMO jobs each wait for a reviewer's approval. The last job marks the release as latest, which updates userscript installs.

A recut after a store rejection needs a new `.N` version, because AMO never reuses a version number.

## Prior art and thanks

No code is copied from any of these projects. Ideas that shaped this one are credited here, and two projects are listed for comparison only.

- [AI warning for Steam](https://github.com/seeeeew/aiwarningforsteam) by seeeeew: the low-permission manifest, separate cache lifetimes for positive and negative results, and the idea of an automated check for heading changes.
- [Steam AI Games Indicator](https://github.com/Pierre-Demessence/SteamAIGamesIndicator) by Pierre-Demessence: badging every surface, including wishlist and home capsules, guarding against age gates before trusting a negative, and serial requests with a delay.
- [AI Generated Content Filter for Steam](https://github.com/SoBloxsy/AI-Content-Hider-for-Steam) by SoBloxsy: falling back from hiding to highlighting where hiding breaks a list.
- [Augmented Steam](https://github.com/IsThereAnyDeal/AugmentedSteam): ideas only (handling both classic and React store pages, one module per feature, and the request for a dismissible banner). It is GPL-3.0 licensed, and nothing from it is used in any form.
- [Slop-Inator](https://github.com/Dysnomia-Studio/slopinator) by Dysnomia Studio: listed for comparison. It shaped no part of this project.
- [Enhanced Steam](https://github.com/jshackles/Enhanced_Steam) by Jason Shackles: listed for comparison. Its development ended in 2019, and Augmented Steam continues from it. It is GPL-3.0 licensed, and nothing from it is used in any form.

## How it was built

`docs/adr/0001-detect-disclosure-via-getitems.mdx`:

```mdx
---
status: accepted
date: 2026-10-20
decision-makers: Jorge Rodriguez de la Vega
---

# Detect AI disclosure through GetItems, with an English HTML fallback

## Context and problem statement

The extension and the userscript mark Steam store items whose developers disclosed generative AI use. A page can show dozens of items (a search page has 50 rows). The signal must be read for every app ID on the page, in any store language, without sending anything to a server of the project's own. The disclosure is self-reported; the signal means "the developer disclosed", never "uses AI" or "AI-free" (see [rq3-reliability](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq3-reliability.md)).

How should the core learn, for a set of app IDs, whether each one has a disclosure?

## Decision drivers

- Request count: a 50-row page must cost far fewer than 50 requests, because rate limits are per IP and shared with ordinary browsing ([rq5-extension-constraints](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq5-extension-constraints.md)).
- Resilience: Valve retranslates the disclosure heading (Russian in 2026-02, French in 2026-09); detection must not depend on localized page text ([rq2-data-surface](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq2-data-surface.md)).
- Privacy (project rule 1): app IDs reach only the Valve hosts of the page being browsed, always with `credentials: "omit"`. No seed lists, no analytics, no server of the project's own.
- Honest semantics (project rule 4): three states, and absence of evidence is never shown or stored as "not disclosed".
- Coverage: every surface that carries an app ID, including pages whose app page is age-gated or adult-only.
- Display: the developer's own words, in the page language where the developer translated them.

## Considered options

1. Batched `IStoreBrowseService/GetItems` with `include_extra_details`, plus an English HTML fallback (chosen).
2. Per-app HTML scraping, one page fetch per app with a localized heading table (the pattern of the prior-art extensions, see [rq4-prior-art](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq4-prior-art.md)).
3. A seed list derived from SteamDB or its tag, shipped or downloaded, refreshed on a schedule.
4. English-only GetItems for detection, plus a second call in the store language for the banner.
5. GetItems in English, with English notes everywhere.

## Decision outcome

Chosen option 1. The core asks GetItems for batches of unseen app IDs and falls back to the app page only for IDs the API leaves unknown.

- Primary source: `GET https://api.steampowered.com/IStoreBrowseService/GetItems/v1` with `data_request.include_extra_details: true`. An app is disclosed when `success === 1` and `extra_details.content_survey_ai_notes` is non-empty after trimming whitespace, including `U+200B`. It is not disclosed when `success === 1` and `extra_details` is present without notes. Everything else is unknown. Results are keyed by the requested `id`, never by `appid`, which is `0` for an invalid item ([rq6, spike 2 (S2)](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq6-verification-spikes.md)).
- Batching: one request per batch of up to 50 unseen IDs, none for cached verdicts. IDs are deduplicated first, because the API does not merge duplicates. The practical ceiling is the URL length (250 IDs passed and 300 failed in [rq6, spike 1 (S1)](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq6-verification-spikes.md)). A batch whose encoded URL would exceeds 4,000 characters is split further.
- Page language: `context.language` is the page's Steam language, taken from `<html lang>` through one mapping table owned by core (the same table gives the `auto` locale in [ADR 0004 (i18n message catalogs)](0004-i18n-message-catalogs.mdx)). A language outside the table falls back to `english`. Spike 2 showed that the set of disclosing apps is identical in every language and that only the note text is translated. Detection stays the same, and the banner and tooltips show the developer's translation without a second call. The cached verdict keeps the language its notes came in; the banner re-fetches one app when that differs from the page.
- Fallback: for IDs GetItems left unknown `missing`, at most 10 per page view, one at a time and 1 s apart, the core fetches `/app/<id>/?l=english` with `credentials: "omit"` and parses the English heading. Notes from this path are English. The parser reports unknown `gated` when the final URL is under `/agecheck/` or `/login/`, is not under `/app/<id>`, or the page has no `#appHubAppName` ([rq6, spike 7 (S7)](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq6-verification-spikes.md)). It collects every `#game_area_content_descriptors` (the ID is duplicated by the mature content block) and matches the heading text `AI Generated Content Disclosure`, a detection constant that is never displayed.
- No localized heading table and no seed lists: the heading is matched in English only, on a page requested in English.
- Three states with neutral absence: not disclosed and unknown render nothing. Unknown is never persisted as not disclosed.
- Freshness (tunable constants, recorded here for context): disclosed 7 days, not disclosed 12 hours, unknown `gated` or `missing` 6 hours. `error` and `rate-limited` live in page memory only. Disclosures are added after launch far more often than removed ([rq3-reliability](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq3-reliability.md)), which explains the long positive and short negative TTLs.
- Failure handling: a 200 answer is a batch error when `x-eresult` is present and not `1`, or when `store_items` is missing although IDs were sent. A `TypeError` from `fetch` is treated like a 429, because Valve's error answers carry no CORS headers and reach JavaScript as a bare `TypeError` (spike 1). One persisted circuit breaker backs off for 60 s plus up to 10 s of jitter.

### Consequences

- Good: a 50-row search page costs one request of about 1 to 1.5 s, where per-app scraping costs about 50.
- Good: detection survives Steam retranslating the heading, because it keys on an API field and ignores localized text.
- Good: the API answers for adult-only, delisted and age-gated apps cookie-less (spike 2). The HTML fallback is rarely needed and gated pages are no blind spot.
- Good: the privacy surface is two Valve hosts, cookie-less, and nothing else.
- Bad: GetItems is not part of Valve's documented web API and may change without notice (`rq2-data-surface.md`). Mitigation: the HTML fallback, a live canary before every release, and the userscript as a fast-fix channel while store reviews are pending.
- Bad: the real rate limit is unknown (spike 1 never reached a 429), and a bare `TypeError` also opens the breaker after an ordinary network failure, costing a 60 s pause.
- Bad: the cache keeps notes in the language they were fetched in, so a badge tooltip can show the previous language until the entry expires. The banner re-fetches; tooltips do not.
- Neutral: fallback notes are English even on a localized page.

## Pros and cons of the options

### 1. Batched GetItems with an English HTML fallback

- Good: about one request per page and independent of language; verified first-hand (CORS from the store origin, 50 IDs in one call, duplicates confirmed, same-origin page fetch works).
- Good: the fallback reuses the one thing the API cannot give, the visible page, and needs no localized table.
- Bad: an undocumented endpoint (see consequences).

### 2. Per-app HTML scraping with a localized heading table

- Good: reads exactly what users see; existing tools document the behavior.
- Bad: about 50 requests per search page; the leading extension ships about 33 localized headings and broke when Steam retranslated them (Russian, French and Malay in 2026).
- Bad: age-gated and adult-only pages redirect cookie-less, leaving every such app a blind spot until a fallback exists anyway.

### 3. A seed list

- Good: zero requests at runtime.
- Bad: the only large lists derive from SteamDB, whose FAQ bans scraping and republishing; the reusable `appids.json` inherits that risk ([rq4-prior-art](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq4-prior-art.md)).
- Bad: it goes stale (late disclosures sit below the list's maximum ID until a manual refresh) and needs a remote fetch, which breaks the privacy and no-remote-code rules.

### 4. English GetItems plus a second call for the banner

- Good: cached notes are always English, giving the cache one language.
- Bad: an extra request on every app page, and tooltips stay English. Spike 2 removed the reason for it: presence does not depend on the language.

### 5. English everywhere

- Good: simplest cache.
- Bad: shows English text where the developer wrote a translation. Rejected for the same reason as option 4.

## More information

- Evidence: [rq2-data-surface](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq2-data-surface.md), [rq6-verification-spikes](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq6-verification-spikes.md) (spikes 1, 2 and 7), [steam-ai-disclosure](../research/steam-ai-disclosure.md).
- Related: [ADR 0003 (content-script-only runtime)](0003-content-script-only-runtime.mdx) covers where the request runs; [ADR 0004 (i18n message catalogs)](0004-i18n-message-catalogs.mdx) covers the language mapping.
- Revisit when the canary shows GetItems dropping `include_extra_details`, or when an actual 429 is observed and the real limit is known.

```

status: accepted
date: 2026-10-20
decision-makers: Jorge Rodriguez de la Vega
---

# One framework-free core, thin platform adapters, and a mise-driven toolchain

## Context and problem statement

The product ships three artifacts: a Chrome MV3 extension, a Firefox MV3 extension and a Tampermonkey/Violentmonkey userscript. They must behave identically, be reviewable by AMO staff who rebuild from source, and follow the project rules on strict typing, formatting, efficiency and a single toolchain manager (rules 5, 10, 11, 14 and 15 in the root `AGENTS.md`).

How is the code organized, and which build, check and test tools carry it? Spike 8 (S8) measured the tool choices ([rq7-library-study](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq7-library-study.md)).

## Decision drivers

- One behavior, three targets: no logic duplicated per platform.
- Reviewability: bundles are not minified (rule 2) and AMO reviewers rebuild them.
- Strict static typing without escape hatches: no `any`, no assertions, `unknown` until validated (rule 10).
- Bundle budgets: `content.js` at most 118 KB and the userscript at most 80 KB, unminified (rule 13).
- One toolchain manager and task runner, identical on Windows and Linux, local and CI (rule 14).
- Few moving parts, with maintained, permissively licensed dependencies (rule 12).

## Considered options

### Architecture

1. Framework-free core plus two thin adapters (chosen): `src/core` depends only on ports; `src/platform/extension` and `src/platform/userscript` are the only shipped composition roots.
2. A framework such as WXT for the extension plus a second plugin for the userscript, with logic spread across entry points.
3. Two separate codebases.

### Toolchain (each row weighed in rq7)

| Concern          | Chosen                                                             | Alternatives weighed                                            |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Bundling         | esbuild 0.28 CLI driven by `scripts/build.py`, one call per target | WXT with vite-plugin-monkey; plain Vite with vite-plugin-monkey |
| Type check       | TypeScript 7 `tsc --noEmit`                                        | TypeScript 6 `tsc`                                              |
| Lint             | oxlint with type-aware rules and one own `jsPlugins` rule          | typescript-eslint presets; Biome                                |
| Format           | dprint 0.64, seven plugins, `.mdx` association                     | Biome plus Prettier                                             |
| Validation       | valibot 1.5                                                        | zod 4 mini; hand-written guards                                 |
| Tests            | vitest 5 with happy-dom                                            | jsdom as default                                                |
| Extension types  | `@types/chrome`, no polyfill                                       | `chrome-types`; `webextension-polyfill`                         |
| Userscript types | hand-written `gm.d.ts`                                             | `@violentmonkey/types`; `@types/tampermonkey`                   |
| Workflows        | actionlint plus zizmor                                             | actionlint alone                                                |
| Package manager  | pnpm from mise, `pmOnFail: error`                                  | none                                                            |

## Decision outcome

Chosen: option 1 for the architecture, and every "Chosen" cell above for the toolchain.

### Architecture

- `src/core` uses only DOM and web standards and never names `chrome`, `browser` or `GM` (rule 5). `tsconfig.core.json` sets `"types": []` and never includes `gm.d.ts`; a platform name in core fails the type check.
- Core depends on small ports (`Http`, `KeyValueStore`, `Clock`, `Logger`, `SettingsSource`, `MessageCatalog`). Every implementation passes the shared contract tests. The extension content script and the userscript `main.ts` are the only shipped roots; `src/platform/dev/inject.ts` is a dev-only root that is never packaged.
- New store surfaces are new placement entries and new detection sources are new detector links; the scanner and the chain are not edited for them (rule 11). See `src/core/AGENTS.md`.

### Toolchain, with the reasons rq7 found

- esbuild: one package with no JavaScript dependencies, builds several IIFE entries, and gives byte-stable output for the same inputs and version. `--banner:js` applies to every entry of a call; the userscript header goes on the userscript call only. WXT carries a large transitive tree that AMO reviewers would rebuild; plain Vite's library mode refuses multiple IIFE entries. Costs: a hand-written userscript header and manifest overlays (both covered by checks) and no HMR (esbuild watch with `web-ext run` reloads Firefox; Chrome is reloaded by hand).
- TypeScript 7: GA since 2026-07-08 and the npm `latest`; about 2.3 times faster on the sample with identical diagnostics. It ships no programmatic API, which matters only to typescript-eslint. It defaults `types` to `[]`; every tsconfig lists its ambient packages explicitly. Scripts test for a non-zero exit and ignore the specific code.
- oxlint with type-aware rules: covers every required rule, including `consistent-type-assertions` with `assertionStyle: "never"`, runs about 5 times faster, and works on TypeScript 7 directly, whereas typescript-eslint caps `typescript` below 6.1. oxlint has no `no-restricted-syntax`. A 12-line project rule in `lint/restricted-syntax.mjs` (loaded through `jsPlugins`, run at lint time, never bundled) turns ESQuery selectors into the literal-flow reports that enforce rule 9. `ban-ts-comment` is set with `"ts-expect-error": true`. Biome was rejected: it has no `no-unsafe-*` family. Documented fallback if the alpha JS plugin API proves flaky: typescript-eslint with the alias pair `typescript` as `npm:@typescript/typescript6` and `@typescript/native` as `npm:typescript@7`, which keeps the type check on TypeScript 7. rq7 called this a close call, and maturity is the argument for the fallback.
- dprint: Biome formats no Markdown, YAML or TOML, and Prettier's MDX parser turned `2 * 3 * 4` into `2 _ 3 _ 4`. dprint skips `.mdx` silently unless `"markdown": { "associations": ["**/*.{md,mdx}"] }` is set; with it, ADRs are formatted safely with `textWrap: "maintain"`. It parses MDX as CommonMark, which keeps JSX blocks in docs simple.
- valibot: 10.8 KB unminified for the GetItems schema against 37.3 KB for zod mini, which alone would use 62 percent of the content-script budget. Use `v.exactOptional`, `v.readonly()` on every nested object, and validate each `store_items` entry on its own, because one malformed item rejects a whole-response schema in all three implementations tried. Hand-written guards stay the fallback if the size budget ever fails.
- vitest with happy-dom: both DOMs passed the needed APIs; happy-dom starts faster and implements `innerText`, observers, `popover` and `dialog`, which jsdom 30 lacks. jsdom is a per-file cross-check only.
- `@types/chrome` without a polyfill: it keeps storage values `unknown`, where `chrome-types` uses `any`. The platform wrapper is `"browser" in globalThis ? globalThis.browser : globalThis.chrome`, because `globalThis.browser ?? globalThis.chrome` fails `no-unnecessary-condition`. The polyfill is stale and takes about 64 percent of the content-script budget. The type argument of `storage.local.get<T>()` is never used, since it is an unchecked assertion.
- Hand-written `gm.d.ts`: neither `@violentmonkey/types` nor `@types/tampermonkey` compiles under `skipLibCheck: false` plus `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, and both type `GM.getValue<T>` as an unchecked assertion. The project file declares exactly the granted APIs with `unknown` returns; signatures follow the manager documentation and no declaration text is copied.
- actionlint plus zizmor: zizmor audits the secret-holding release workflows (template injection, permissions, unpinned actions) and runs offline in `lint`, which leaves `prepush` without a GitHub token.
- pnpm from mise: without `pmOnFail: error` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, pnpm 12 silently downloads and runs the version named in `packageManager`, outside mise (proven in rq7). A check compares the two pins.
- mise is the only manager and runner (rule 14). Hooks come from `mise generate git-pre-commit` and run `mise run precommit` and `mise run prepush`. Tasks call scripts rather than inline shell, because mise runs inline strings with `cmd /c` on Windows. Tools without a registry entry carry backend prefixes (`"npm:web-ext"`, `"pypi:mypy"`). Libraries imported from `node_modules` (esbuild, TypeScript, oxlint, valibot, vitest, happy-dom) are exact-pinned in `package.json` and the lockfile, not in `mise.toml`.
- Open item from rq7 row 14, settled here: Node stays at 24.14.0 (the AMO reviewer environment), although 24.22.0 is the latest 24.x. `uv` is pinned in `mise.toml`, which makes the `pypi` backend install mypy the same way on CI and on a clean reviewer machine (the no-uv path was not tested). `mise.lock` is committed when the toolchain step can generate it with matching entries on Windows and Linux; if it cannot, the lock is dropped and this ADR is amended, never silently skipped.
- AMO build from source: install mise (one documented command), then run `mise install` and `mise run build`. If a reviewer objects to mise, the documented fallback is the same `build.py` run with a stock Python and pnpm.

### Consequences

- Good: one behavior and one test suite for three targets; the compiler checks that core is platform-free.
- Good: the strictest typing available for storage and network boundaries, with the cheapest validation library.
- Good: a single command set locally, in hooks and in CI.
- Bad: oxlint JS plugins are alpha, and the literal-flow rule depends on them staying compatible with ESLint's `create(context)`; the typescript-eslint alias fallback costs a larger dependency tree.
- Bad: the hand-written userscript header, manifest overlays and `gm.d.ts` need upkeep against the managers; checks cover header and grants.
- Bad: AMO reviewers must install mise; a long Windows checkout path can hit the 260-character limit that failed every install in the rq7 proof.
- Bad: dprint does not parse MDX natively, so complex JSX in docs could be reformatted badly; `fmt-check` in `prepush` shows any change.

## Pros and cons of the options

### Architecture

- Core plus adapters: good (one logic, small adapters, enforceable purity); bad (ports add indirection that tests and contracts must police).
- WXT plus vite-plugin-monkey: good (HMR, manifest generation); bad (two frameworks and configs around one core, WXT conventions leak into core, large tree for AMO to rebuild).
- Two codebases: bad (drift, doubled tests); rejected outright.

## More information

- Evidence: [rq7-library-study](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq7-library-study.md) (rows 1 to 14) and the plan's "Tooling decisions".
- Related: [ADR 0001 (detect disclosure via GetItems)](0001-detect-disclosure-via-getitems.mdx), [ADR 0003 (content-script-only runtime)](0003-content-script-only-runtime.mdx), [ADR 0005 (release pipeline)](0005-release-pipeline.mdx).

# Content-script-only runtime with no background script and no host permissions

## Context and problem statement

Detection ([ADR 0001 (detect disclosure via GetItems)](0001-detect-disclosure-via-getitems.mdx)) calls `api.steampowered.com`, a different origin from the store pages the extension runs on. Extension code that makes cross-origin calls usually needs either `host_permissions` or a background script that relays the request. Both widen the store review surface (Chrome's limited-use rules, AMO's data collection declaration) and the permission prompt users see. The earlier research assumed a background relay would be needed ([rq5-extension-constraints](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq5-extension-constraints.md)) and left Firefox content-script behavior untested.

Where does the GetItems request run, and what permissions does that require?

## Decision drivers

- The smallest permission set: `storage` plus content-script matches on `https://store.steampowered.com/*` (project rule 3).
- Privacy (project rule 1): requests cookie-less, only to the Valve hosts of the page being browsed.
- Identical behavior in Chrome and Firefox, and in the userscript.
- No service-worker lifecycle: Chrome kills workers after 30 s idle and they have no DOM.
- A small, quickly reviewable AMO and Chrome Web Store submission.

## Considered options

1. Content script only (chosen): the content script calls GetItems with plain `fetch`; no background script and no `host_permissions`.
2. Background relay for `api.steampowered.com`: the content script messages a background script that fetches, with `host_permissions: ["https://api.steampowered.com/*"]`.
3. Relay for Firefox only, content script for Chrome (the branch the first plan kept open until the spikes ran).

## Decision outcome

Chosen option 1. The manifest has `permissions: ["storage"]`, one content script matching `https://store.steampowered.com/*`, no `host_permissions` and no `background` key. A build check asserts all three.

Evidence from the step 2 spikes ([rq6-verification-spikes](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq6-verification-spikes.md)):

- Spike 3 (S3), CORS: GetItems CORS is an allow-list of Valve origins (it does not answer `*`). Store and community pages read it (200, `type: "cors"`); a foreign origin (wikipedia.org) gets a `TypeError`. `x-eresult` is exposed to JavaScript. Only a host permission would make a response readable to a request that carries an extension origin.
- Spike 4 (S4), extension fetch: a throwaway MV3 extension with no permissions and one store content script read GetItems with plain `fetch` in Chrome 155 and in Firefox Nightly 160 (`type: "cors"`, 200, `x-eresult` readable), and fetched the same-origin app page. `content.fetch` does not exist in an MV3 content script and is not used. Given spike 3, a readable `cors` answer means both browsers sent the request with the store page's origin.
- Spike 6 (S6), userscripts: Tampermonkey 5.5 on Chrome and Firefox Nightly runs the same plain `fetch` with no `@connect`, which gives the userscript the same path.

### Consequences

- Good: with no `host_permissions` and no background script, the install prompt, the store review and the permission justification stay minimal, and Firefox can declare `data_collection_permissions: {required: ["none"]}`.
- Good: no worker lifecycle, no message passing, one code path for extension and userscript.
- Good: HTML parsing stays in the content script, where a DOM exists.
- Bad: the result depends on browsers continuing to send content-script requests with the page origin. This is inferred from the readable `cors` answer; the request header itself was not inspected (rq6 caveat). If a browser changes this, requests fail as a `TypeError`, which the circuit breaker treats like a rate limit, and the live canary would not catch it because it runs outside a browser. Mitigation: the manual checklist runs on Chrome and Firefox before each release.
- Bad: Valve could narrow the CORS allow-list. Then this ADR is revisited with option 2, accepting a new permission.
- Bad: error answers carry no CORS headers, so a status and `Retry-After` are never readable (spike 1); the throttle uses a fixed backoff.
- Neutral: Violentmonkey was not tested (spike 6); it goes on the manual checklist.

## Pros and cons of the options

### 1. Content script only

- Good: smallest permission set, verified in both browsers and in Tampermonkey.
- Bad: relies on page-origin behavior (see above).

### 2. Background relay

- Good: independent of content-script origin behavior, because host permissions lift CORS for extension pages.
- Bad: adds `host_permissions` for `api.steampowered.com` (a scarier prompt and more review text), a background lifecycle (service worker in Chrome, event page in Firefox), and a message hop for every batch. The userscript still needs a different path, and the two targets diverge.

### 3. Firefox-only relay

- Good: would cover the case where Firefox content scripts failed CORS.
- Bad: spike 4 showed Firefox works without it, which leaves the extra permission without benefit. Dropped.

## More information

- Evidence: [rq6-verification-spikes](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq6-verification-spikes.md) (spikes 3, 4 and 6), [rq5-extension-constraints](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq5-extension-constraints.md).
- Related: [ADR 0001 (detect disclosure via GetItems)](0001-detect-disclosure-via-getitems.mdx), [ADR 0002 (single codebase and tooling)](0002-single-codebase-and-tooling.mdx). Changing this runtime needs a new ADR (project rule 3, permissions).

# Message catalogs in Chrome messages.json with a small core runtime

## Context and problem statement

Project rule 9 (i18n from day 1) requires every user-visible or logged message (UI copy, errors, warnings, notices, ARIA labels, tooltips, manifest and userscript names and descriptions) to live in a keyed, typed message catalog. English and Spanish ship in v1, and adding a language must take a catalog drop with no code change. The same strings are needed in three places: the extension manifest (`__MSG_*__`), the framework-free core, and the userscript header, which has no browser i18n API at all.

The target locale follows the Steam page language on store pages, because that is the language the user reads. The developer's disclosure text is data, shown verbatim and never translated.

What format and runtime do the catalogs use?

## Decision drivers

- Works in the core (no browser API), in the extension and in the userscript.
- Follows the Steam page language at runtime, beyond the browser UI language.
- Typed keys and placeholders: a missing key or a wrong placeholder fails the type check.
- Translation tooling: Crowdin and Weblate read the format without conversion.
- Small: the content script has a 60 KB unminified budget, shared with the validation library.
- One authored source of truth.

## Considered options

1. `chrome.i18n` with `_locales` only.
2. i18next (or a similar full library).
3. ICU MessageFormat through `@formatjs/intl-messageformat`.
4. Chrome `messages.json` as the single authored format, plus a dependency-free core runtime of about 60 lines (chosen).

## Decision outcome

Chosen option 4.

- Format: `src/locales/<lang>/messages.json` in Chrome `messages.json` format is the only authored source. The extension needs it for `__MSG_*__` manifest strings (name, description, action title), and Crowdin and Weblate read it directly. Keys are snake_case grouped by prefix (`badge_`, `banner_`, `options_`, `error_`, `warn_`, `notice_`, `ext_`, `userscript_`). Every message carries a `description` for translators.
- Runtime: `createI18n(catalogs, locale)`, `t(key, params)` and `plural(baseKey, count, params)` live in core and use no browser API. They substitute `$placeholder$` values, resolve plurals through `_one` and `_other` key suffixes with `Intl.PluralRules`, and fall back to English for a missing key or locale.
- Typed keys: a generator script turns the English catalog into `keys.gen.ts` (a `MessageKey` union and per-key placeholder types), and `t("missing_key")` or a wrong placeholder fails `tsc`. Errors carry a `code` that is a `MessageKey` plus typed params, with no prose; the logger takes keys.
- Locale resolution: the `locale` setting defaults to `auto`. On store pages `auto` follows `<html lang>` mapped through the table recorded in [research note 6 (verification spikes), spike 5](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq6-verification-spikes.md); for example `en` is `english`, `es-419` is `latam`, `pt-br` is `brazilian`, `zh-cn` is `schinese`. Elsewhere it follows `navigator.language`. A locale without a catalog falls back to English. The same table read in reverse gives GetItems its `context.language` ([ADR 0001 (detect disclosure via GetItems)](0001-detect-disclosure-via-getitems.mdx)), and one core module owns it.
- Build: the build copies catalogs to `_locales/<lang>/messages.json` for the extension and inlines them into the userscript bundle. The userscript `@name` and `@description` come from the English catalog, plus `@name:<lang>` and `@description:<lang>` for every other shipped locale.
- Enforcement: a check script verifies that every locale has the same keys and placeholders as English, that every catalog key is used and that every message has a `description`. The literal-flow lint rule (string literals into `textContent`, `title`, `aria-*`, `console.*`, `new Error`) catches hardcoded copy; allowed literals are identifiers, selectors, URLs, storage keys, CSS class names and detection constants. The same check script fails when catalog text of any shipped locale appears as a string literal under `src/` or `tests/`, so tests take their expected text from `t(key, params)` or the catalog JSON; `tests/locales/` and `tests/fixtures/` are exempt. A test also fails if any catalog message contains "uses AI", "AI-free" or "no AI" (project rule 4, semantics).

### Consequences

- Good: one authored format feeds the manifest, the core and the userscript header; translators use standard tooling.
- Good: roughly 60 lines of project code and no runtime dependency; the content-script budget stays free for logic.
- Good: typed keys make an untranslated or misspelled key a compile error.
- Bad: no ICU select or nested plural syntax; complex grammar (gender, nested plurals) cannot be expressed. Acceptable for badge, banner and options copy; revisit if a language needs it (option 3 is the upgrade path, since the catalog keys stay the same).
- Bad: the project owns the plural and placeholder code and its tests, including a test-only pseudo-locale for fallback, plural and placeholder handling.
- Bad: layouts must tolerate translations about 40 percent longer, and badge text truncates with the full message in `title`.
- Neutral: English and Spanish are the shipped locales in v1; right-to-left layouts and a translation platform are on the roadmap.

## Pros and cons of the options

### 1. `chrome.i18n` with `_locales` only

- Good: zero code, native to the extension.
- Bad: unavailable in the core and the userscript, and it resolves the browser UI language, so it cannot follow the Steam page language at runtime. Rejected.

### 2. i18next

- Good: mature, rich features.
- Bad: about 40 KB (the figure recorded in the plan) against a 60 KB budget, and its own key conventions, which need a conversion step to produce the `messages.json` the manifest requires.

### 3. ICU MessageFormat through `@formatjs/intl-messageformat`

- Good: rich plurals and selects; a standard syntax.
- Bad: one more dependency for needs the v1 copy does not have, and a second format to convert into `messages.json` for the manifest.

### 4. `messages.json` plus a small runtime

- Good and bad: see consequences.

## More information

- Library check (project rule 12, library check first): unlike the tooling rows, no i18n library was spiked in [rq7-library-study](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq7-library-study.md). The size figure for i18next comes from the plan and is unmeasured. The decision was taken in review on 2026-10-20 for the format-reuse reason, which does not depend on the exact size.
- The `<html lang>` table comes from research note 6, spike 5 (rq6 S5). The i18n runtime lands in the toolchain step, before any feature code.
- Related: [ADR 0001 (detect disclosure via GetItems)](0001-detect-disclosure-via-getitems.mdx), [ADR 0002 (single codebase and tooling)](0002-single-codebase-and-tooling.mdx).

`docs/adr/0005-release-pipeline.mdx`:

# Release pipeline: changie fragments, CalVer, nightly prereleases and manual promotion to the stores

## Context and problem statement

The project ships to the Chrome Web Store, to addons.mozilla.org (AMO) and as a userscript hosted on GitHub releases. The release train this project uses combines changie fragments, CalVer, a bot-made tag, a nightly deploy and prod on manual dispatch of the same tag. Prior art among extensions mostly stops at a GitHub release and uploads to the stores by hand; none of the projects read uses changelog fragments or a two-stage nightly-then-prod promotion ([extension-release-pipeline](../research/extension-release-pipeline.md)).

The store rules constrain what carries over: the manifest version must be unpadded dotted integers, AMO never reuses a version number across channels, and no store offers keyless publishing.

How are versions chosen, releases cut, and artifacts published?

## Decision drivers

- A version string valid in the manifest, the Git tag and the userscript `@version` at once.
- Promote the artifact that was tested; AMO checks that the source rebuilds to the same files.
- A nightly must not burn a version number on the listing that prod publishes to.
- Reviewed, auditable store credentials, with human approval before anything reaches users.
- Low ceremony for a one-person project, and a pipeline thin enough to keep in mise tasks and short scripts (project rule 14, mise is the only toolchain manager).

## Considered options

1. changie fragments, unpadded CalVer, nightly GitHub prereleases, manual prod promotion of the same artifacts (chosen).
2. Manual store uploads from a local build, with a GitHub release (what most prior art does).
3. Rebuild at prod time from the tag, instead of promoting the nightly's artifacts.
4. A signed beta channel (a separate AMO add-on ID and Chrome Web Store listing) fed by every nightly.

## Decision outcome

Chosen option 1, with the release train adapted to the store rules in [rq1-prior-art](../research/extension-release-pipeline/rq1-prior-art.md).

- Fragments: `.changie.yaml` with kinds Added, Changed, Fixed and Removed. A CI gate fails a pull request that changes `src/` without a new `.changes/unreleased/*.yaml`, unless it carries the `no-changelog-fragment` label. The changelog feeds the GitHub release body and AMO's per-version release notes. No Chrome Web Store release-notes field was found.
- Version: unpadded CalVer `YYYY.M.D`, with `.N` (from 1) for a same-day recut: `2026.10.20`, `2026.10.20.1`. Chrome and AMO accept one to four dotted integers with no leading zeros, and `2026.10.05` is invalid. The same string is the Git tag, the manifest `version` and the userscript `@version`. `package.json` holds the last released version; feature changes never edit it (project rule 7, one version source).
- Train: a scheduled workflow at 00:00 UTC (and manual dispatch with a `dry_run` input) finds the newest green commit on `main`, and skips when none is green, a release PR is open, or nothing landed since the last tag. If fragments exist, the release GitHub App opens a batch pull request (`changie batch`, `changie merge`, the `package.json` version) that auto-merges after the required checks. There is no merge queue, because the repository is on a personal account. No fragments means no release.
- Tag: when the batch PR merges, a job creates the tag on the merge commit as the release app. A tag ruleset admits only that app, and events created by an app can trigger workflows where `GITHUB_TOKEN` events cannot. The job then dispatches the nightly workflow with the tag.
- Nightly: validates that the tag is CalVer and sits on `origin/main` with green CI, builds once with the frozen lockfile, runs the reproducibility check, packages, and creates a GitHub prerelease with the version's changelog section and every artifact (Chrome zip, Firefox zip, `.user.js`, `.meta.js`, AMO source zip). Nothing goes to any store. A prerelease does not move `releases/latest`, and userscript users do not update yet.
- Prod: manual dispatch with a `tag` input, run from the tag ref. It downloads the prerelease assets and promotes the same artifacts with no rebuild:
  - GitHub environment `chrome-web-store`: upload and publish through Chrome Web Store API v2 with `chrome-webstore-upload-cli` v4 (which needs a publisher ID).
  - GitHub environment `amo`: `web-ext sign --channel listed` with `--upload-source-code` for the source zip and the changelog section as release notes.
  - Both environments require a reviewer's approval. Credentials are environment secrets; the release app's ID and private key are repository secrets.
  - Last, it marks the GitHub release as latest, which moves `releases/latest/download/<slug>.meta.js` and lets userscript users update.
- Chrome Web Store auth (OAuth refresh token or service account): replaced by [ADR 0007](0007-chrome-web-store-workload-identity.mdx). The research found no keyless option for any store. API v2 (2025-10-15) adds service accounts, which are not tied to a personal Google session; the refresh-token flow works with the CLI today and is the common pattern. Decision: start with an OAuth refresh token in the `chrome-web-store` environment, because it is the path `chrome-webstore-upload-cli` documents and the one with the most field use, and move to a service account when its use from GitHub Actions has been tried by hand (the research lists that test as unverified). Rotation is calendared.
- Userscript URLs: `@updateURL` and `@downloadURL` point at `releases/latest/download/<slug>.meta.js` and `.user.js`. These URLs skip drafts and prereleases.

Sequencing: the changie setup (`.changie.yaml`, `.changes/`) and the pull request changelog gate are being built early, in the toolchain step (plan step 4), so that every pull request from then on carries a fragment. Everything else in this ADR (CalVer computation, the train, the nightly, prod promotion and the store credentials) stays in the release pipeline step (plan step 15).

### Consequences

- Good: the artifact users install is the artifact that was built, reproduced and tested; AMO's rebuild-from-source check sees the same files.
- Good: nightlies cost nothing in the stores and burn no AMO version numbers, because they are GitHub prereleases only.
- Good: a human approval gates each store, and the changelog is written at change time.
- Good: the userscript has a fast-fix channel that does not wait for store review.
- Bad: long-lived store secrets that must be rotated; no store offers OIDC.
- Bad: a recut after a store rejection needs a new version (`.N`), because AMO never reuses one, even after deletion.
- Bad: Chrome Web Store API v2 from GitHub Actions with these credentials is untested; v1.1 support was announced to end on 2026-10-15, and `chrome-webstore-upload-cli` v3 may no longer work.
- Bad: testers get no automatic updates between prods; they install the prerelease by hand.
- Neutral: out of scope for v1: Edge, staged and partial rollout (needs more than 10,000 weekly users), Greasy Fork mirroring, a signed beta channel and localized store listings. All are on the roadmap.

## Pros and cons of the options

### 1. Fragments, CalVer, prerelease nightly, manual promotion

- Good and bad: see consequences. No extension prior art uses it, but nothing in the store rules contradicts it.

### 2. Manual store uploads

- Good: nothing to build or secure; the common practice.
- Bad: error-prone, unreviewed, and the version, tag and changelog drift apart. Rejected for a project that must also ship a userscript from the same tag.

### 3. Rebuild at prod time

- Good: simpler workflow graph.
- Bad: the store artifact may differ from the one tested, and AMO verifies source against build output. Promoting one artifact removes that risk.

### 4. A signed beta channel

- Good: testers auto-update.
- Bad: a second AMO add-on ID and Chrome listing to maintain, review and secure. Deferred to the roadmap; a GitHub prerelease is enough for now.

## Amendment 2026-10-21: as built

The release app is a GitHub App owned by a personal account and installed only on `jrv97/steam-ai-reporter`. The workflows read its ID and key from the repository secrets `RELEASE_APP_ID` and `RELEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` through `actions/create-github-app-token`. The app opens the batch PR, which lets CI run on it, and the tag ruleset admits only this app.

The Chrome Web Store job gets a 15-minute access token through Workload Identity Federation and a service account, and `scripts/cws.py` calls API v2 with it. [ADR 0007](0007-chrome-web-store-workload-identity.mdx) records that choice and the options it replaced.

changie accepts only SemVer, and `changie merge` drops any version file named `YYYY.M.D.N`. For a recut, `scripts/release.py` runs `changie batch YYYY.M.D+N` and renames the file and its heading. It then writes `CHANGELOG.md` from `header.tpl.md` and the version files, newest first.

The tag job runs on `workflow_run` of `ci` for pushes to `main` whose commit message starts with `chore(release): `. CI has passed on the commit before the job tags it, and the nightly's CI check needs no wait loop. The job reads one commit and its parent. A comment on the trigger gives this reason for suppressing zizmor's `dangerous-triggers` finding.

The first version goes to each store by hand. Chrome Web Store API v2 cannot create an item, and AMO needs listing metadata that the release job does not send. The first prerelease's assets are uploaded in each developer dashboard, and that release is marked latest with `gh release edit <tag> --prerelease=false --latest`. Later versions go through the prod workflow.

## More information

- Research: [extension-release-pipeline](../research/extension-release-pipeline.md) and [rq1-prior-art](../research/extension-release-pipeline/rq1-prior-art.md). Items it lists as unverified and that this ADR relies on: Chrome Web Store API v2 from CI with a service account, and Greasy Fork sync (not adopted).
- Related: [ADR 0002 (single codebase and tooling)](0002-single-codebase-and-tooling.mdx) (mise tasks, zizmor on the workflows, reproducible builds).

# The full badge reads "AI use disclosed"

## Context and problem statement

Project rule 4 fixed the full badge's wording as "Discloses AI use". The label has no subject, so on a search row it reads as if the game itself were disclosing something. A plainer label was wanted, and "This game uses AI" was considered among others. Which wording should the full badge carry?

## Decision drivers

- The badge reports a developer's self-disclosure, not a verified fact about the game (rule 4, [rq3-reliability](../research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq3-reliability.md)).
- Disclosures range from live generated content to one upscaled texture, and some say AI was barely used or later removed. The label has to stay true for all of them.
- The copy test rejects "uses AI", "AI-free" and "no AI" in every catalog.
- One line at 11px, with room for longer translations.
- A plain label on a row, close to the compact badge's "AI disclosed".

## Considered options

1. Keep "Discloses AI use".
2. "This game uses AI".
3. "AI use disclosed".

## Decision outcome

Chosen option 3, "AI use disclosed". It says what happened (the use was disclosed), stays attributive, passes the copy test, and pairs with "AI disclosed" on cover images. Rule 4 now names "AI use disclosed" as the wording, and "uses AI" and "AI-free" stay forbidden. The banner keeps the full sentence, "The developer discloses AI use", and the tooltip still quotes the developer.

### Consequences

- Good: plainer to scan on a row, and the same width in the store font (about 82px of text).
- Neutral: "disclosed" names no agent; the banner and the tooltip name the developer.
- The catalog key stays `badge_full`; only its message and translator note change.

## Pros and cons of the options

### Keep "Discloses AI use"

- Good: already used across the specs, the store listing draft and the test guides.
- Bad: no subject, so it reads as if the game discloses.

### "This game uses AI"

- Bad: states a self-report as fact, which is wrong for disclosures that describe little use or use that was removed.
- Bad: breaks rule 4 and fails the copy test.
- Bad: "This game" repeats what the row already shows.

### "AI use disclosed"

- Good: attributive, true for every disclosure, and short.
- Bad: passive; the agent is implied rather than named.

`docs/adr/0007-chrome-web-store-workload-identity.mdx`:

```mdx
---
status: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
decision-makers: Jorge Rodriguez de la Vega
---

# Chrome Web Store publishing authenticates through Workload Identity Federation

## Context and problem statement

The prod workflow uploads the Chrome zip and submits it for review through Chrome Web Store API v2. The API takes a Google OAuth access token with the `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/chromewebstore` scope. [ADR 0005](0005-release-pipeline.mdx) started with an OAuth refresh token stored in the `chrome-web-store` environment. That token lives until revoked, belongs to a personal Google login, and lapses after about six months without use. Prod runs rarely, which makes the last point likely.

How does the Chrome job get its access token?

## Decision drivers

- No long-lived Google credential stored in GitHub.
- Only a release run of this repository can obtain a token.
- Nothing to rotate or renew on a calendar.
- The code we own stays small enough to unit test.

## Considered options

1. **Workload Identity Federation to a service account** (chosen).
2. **OAuth refresh token** for a personal Google account, used through `chrome-webstore-upload-cli` 4.
3. **Service account JSON key** stored as an environment secret.

## Decision outcome

Chosen option 1.

A Google Cloud service account with no IAM roles is added under Settings > Service account in the Chrome Web Store developer dashboard. A publisher can register one service account.

A workload identity pool has a GitHub OIDC provider that maps `google.subject` to the token's `sub`. Its attribute condition admits a token only when `repository_id` is `1426952065` (`jrv97/steam-ai-reporter`), `ref` starts with `refs/tags/`, and `environment` is `chrome-web-store`. Only the subject `repo:jrv97@60591482/steam-ai-reporter@1426952065:environment:chrome-web-store` holds `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` on the service account.

The repository's `sub` claim uses GitHub's immutable form, which names the owner and the repository by numeric ID. `gh api repos/jrv97/steam-ai-reporter/actions/oidc/customization/sub` shows its prefix. A binding written with the plain `repo:jrv97/steam-ai-reporter:environment:chrome-web-store` subject did not match in the first prod run, and the job failed with `iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken` denied.

The Chrome job asks for `id-token: write`. `google-github-actions/auth` 3.0.0 exchanges the GitHub OIDC token for an access token that lasts 15 minutes, with the Chrome Web Store scope, and writes no credentials file.

`scripts/cws.py` makes the API calls with the Python standard library: upload the zip, call `fetchStatus` while the upload is `IN_PROGRESS` (at most 60 checks, 5 seconds apart), then `publish`. Unit tests drive these paths through a fake API.

The `chrome-web-store` environment holds four variables and no secrets: `CWS_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_PROVIDER`, `CWS_SERVICE_ACCOUNT`, `CWS_PUBLISHER_ID` and `CWS_EXTENSION_ID`. None of them grants access on its own.

### Consequences

- Good: GitHub stores no Google secret, so none can leak, expire or need rotation.
- Good: a token lasts 15 minutes, and Google issues one only to a release tag run in this repository's `chrome-web-store` environment.
- Good: `chrome-webstore-upload-cli` leaves `mise.toml`, one pinned tool fewer.
- Bad: Chrome's service account page documents impersonation and key files but does not mention Workload Identity Federation. The first prod run (2026.10.22) tested this path and it worked once the binding used the immutable subject.
- Bad: Google applies an IAM change after a few minutes. A run right after a binding change can still fail with the 403 above, so re-run only the failed job.
- Bad: about 70 lines of API client and tests to maintain, where a CLI maintained elsewhere did the same job.
- Bad: a one-time Google Cloud setup (pool, provider, service account, IAM binding).
- Neutral: AMO has no equivalent. Its JWT keys stay as secrets in the `amo` environment.

## Pros and cons of the options

### 2. OAuth refresh token

- Good: works with a maintained CLI and has the most field use.
- Bad: three long-lived secrets, tied to a personal Google login.
- Bad: lapses after about six months unused, and after 7 days while the consent screen is in testing status.

### 3. Service account key

- Good: not tied to a personal login.
- Bad: a long-lived private key in GitHub, a risk Chrome's own service account page warns about.
- Bad: needs rotation, and an RS256 JWT exchange that the Python standard library cannot sign.

## More information

- Chrome Web Store service accounts: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/service-accounts
- Chrome Web Store API v2 reference: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/api/reference/rest
- This ADR replaces the Chrome Web Store auth choice in [ADR 0005](0005-release-pipeline.mdx).

```
