`docs/research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq3-reliability.md`:

```md
# RQ3: How complete and reliable is Steam's AI content disclosure as a signal?

Researched 2026-10-20. All web fetches were summarised by a small model; where a page could not be fetched (403, truncated) the claim is tagged `search-summary` or `unverified`. No analysis of Steam AI disclosure by Ian Cheng was found; the Totally Human analyses are by Ichiro Lambe (see sources).

## Answer in short

- The disclosure is a self-reported, unaudited floor: it is a lower bound on AI in shipped content, and Valve's January 2026 rewrite exempts AI dev tools ("efficiency gains"). The signal can never mean "this game used no AI".
- Scale: about 1,000 disclosing games (Apr 2024), 7,818 (Jul 2025, ~7%), 10,258 (Nov 2025, ~8%), more than 15,000 games and software on SteamDB (Feb 2026), ~9,400 flagged in a 53,597-release census (Jul 2026); share of new releases 10.9% (2024), 19.9% (2025), 30.8% (2026 to date).
- Concrete gaps exist and are named: The Alters (no disclosure), Crimson Desert (disclosure added after launch), Black Ops 6 (disclosure about a year after launch), retroactive flags (22% of significant-revenue AI games, per one census), vague wording; no case was found of Valve delisting an existing game for non-disclosure.
- Debate: Tim Sweeney called labels senseless (X post, late Nov 2025) and "really irresponsible of Valve" (PC Gamer interview, reported 25 Jun 2026); no Valve response found; as of 2026-10-20 the requirement is still in force, last rewritten in January 2026 (narrower and still in force), and no native Steam filter or tag exists as of the latest coverage found (June 2026).
- For the extension: expect many false negatives (exempt tooling, late or missing disclosures, strategic omission) and some false positives (minor, peripheral or since-removed use; negated text such as "we do NOT use AI-generated art"); label it "discloses AI" and avoid "uses AI" and "AI-free"; community signals (review text, SteamDB tag) are noisy and mostly derived from the same disclosure.

## Findings

### 1. How many Steam games disclose AI, and the trend 2024 to 2026

Timeline of counts (each row has a different scope and method; rows are not strictly comparable):

- 2024-01-10: Valve adds an AI disclosure section to the Steamworks Content Survey, split into pre-generated and live-generated, and says it will show much of it on Steam pages (source: https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/steam-pages-will-now-disclose-which-games-use-ai-generated-content/).
- 2024-04-24: Totally Human media (Ichiro Lambe) ran a script over the store "about" sections and found 1,000 games with a genai disclosure, about ten times what he expected (source: https://totallyhuman.io/blog/the-surprising-number-of-steam-games-that-use-genai). The 2025 post puts this at about 1.1% of the library (source: https://totallyhuman.io/blog/the-surprising-new-number-of-genai-games-on-steam).
- 2025-02-25: SteamDB launches an automatic "AI Content Disclosed" user tag derived from store-page disclosures (source: https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2025/02/steamdb-now-lets-you-filter-out-steam-games-with-ai-generation/; SteamDB's own announcement: https://x.com/SteamDB/status/1894080893632884820, seen only as a search result title). A ">4,900 games at launch" figure appeared in a search summary only: unverified.
- 2025-07-13: 7,818 of about 114,126 games (~7%) disclose; a little under 20% of 2025 releases; ~60% of disclosures are visual asset generation; counts come from Steam's API via the author's "We Love Every Game" platform (source: https://totallyhuman.io/blog/the-surprising-new-number-of-genai-games-on-steam). VGC reported this on 2025-07-17 as "up 800%" from about 1,000 a year earlier (source: https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/steam-games-disclosing-generative-ai-use-are-up-800-this-year/).
- 2025-10-21: 12,284 games carry a disclosure per SteamDB (source: https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2025/10/want-to-avoid-ai-gen-on-steam-this-browser-userscript-might-save-your-day/). The same month's Next Fest: 504 demos, 17% of the event, per a PCGamesN article dated 2025-10-21 (source: https://www.pcgamesn.com/steam/next-fest-generative-ai; the fetch summary attributed the tally to techraptor; attribution is unclear).
- 2025-11-06: Totally Human counts 10,258 titles (~8% of Steam), estimated combined gross about $660 million (Boxleiter estimate, described by the author as the roughest calculation) (source: https://totallyhuman.io/blog/games-with-ai-disclosures-have-grossed-an-estimated-660m-on-steam). The gap to SteamDB's 12,284 two weeks earlier is plausibly scope (SteamDB counts "games and software"), but no source states the reason: unverified.
- 2026-02-12: "more than 15,000 games and software" carry the label per a SteamDB search; Steam itself publishes no total (source: https://stuff.co.za/2026/02/12/are-video-game-developers-using-ai-players-want-to-know-but-the-rules-are-patchy/, a republication of a piece from The Conversation by Thomas Byers and Bjorn Nansen).
- 2026-06-15/16 (June Next Fest): 1,694 of 8,682 event items carry the AI disclosure tag on SteamDB (~19.5%), per a ResetEra thread linking the SteamDB lists (source: https://www.resetera.com/threads/steam-next-fest-has-over-8-600-demos-and-almost-1700-of-them-have-ai-disclosures.1551832/); Eurogamer's count of 1,704 of 8,700 (19.5%) was relayed by Engadget on 2026-06-16 (source: https://engadget.com/2195840/around-a-fifth-of-steam-next-fest-demos-have-a-generative-ai-disclosure). The 10-vs-9 difference is probably snapshot timing; unverified. PCGamesN found 10 of the top 100 demos by popularity carry a disclosure, per a secondary aggregator (source: https://letsdatascience.com/news/over-1000-steam-next-fest-games-disclose-generative-ai-6c11ab90). A PC Gamer figure of 551 of 4,397 SteamDB products was seen only in a search summary and uses a different list: unverified.
- 2026-07-13: Sulka Haro's census (Substack "fragwyz") of 53,597 "Games" releases from mid-2023 to mid-2026 found about 9,400 AI-flagged; roughly one in three new games flagged by mid-2026; flagged launches rose from about 13 per month before the mandate to about 530; 60 to 90 percent of growth in monthly releases is AI-flagged; the 50% crossing in 2027 or 2028 is a scenario and no forecast (source: https://fragwyz.substack.com/p/three-years-of-ai-on-steam). Per-year shares of 10.9% (2024), 19.9% (2025) and 30.8% (2026 to date) are given by secondary coverage (source: https://app.cinevva.com/news/2026-07-20-steam-ai-disclosure-study); the Substack fetch said yearly figures are approximations read from monthly charts; treat them as +/- a few points. PC Gamer covered the census (Shaun Prescott's "Steam week in review" column; page itself not readable, headline seen in search results: https://www.pcgamer.com/gaming-industry/steam-week-in-review-take-cover-because-it-looks-like-more-than-half-of-steam-games-will-have-an-ai-disclosure-by-2027-2028/).
- Method note from Haro: the census enumerates Steam search results and checks each store page for the "AI Generated Content Disclosure" section; flag timing comes from Wayback snapshots (source: https://fragwyz.substack.com/p/three-years-of-ai-on-steam).

Trend in one line: roughly 1% of the catalog in April 2024, 7% in July 2025, 8% in November 2025; among new releases about 7% at the February 2024 start, about 20% in 2025, about 30% in 2026 (sources as above). The flag is binary and does not measure how much AI was used (source: https://fragwyz.substack.com/p/three-years-of-ai-on-steam).

Valve statements: Valve publishes no count. What it has said is in the Steamworks Content Survey docs (AI content section: pre-generated and live-generated; "efficiency gains through the use of these tools is not the focus of this section"; live-generated must describe guardrails; live-generated AI adult only sexual content not wanted "at this time") (source: https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/gettingstarted/contentsurvey). No Valve comment on the Next Fest figures appeared in the engadget piece (source: https://engadget.com/2195840/around-a-fifth-of-steam-next-fest-demos-have-a-generative-ai-disclosure).

### 2. Known gaps, with named examples

Structural gaps in the rules

- January 2026 rewrite (reported 2026-01-16 to 2026-01-20): the form now covers AI content "consumed by players" (art, audio, localization, narrative, marketing, store page, community assets); AI-powered dev tools such as code helpers need no disclosure; examples given are using ChatGPT to check code or an image generator to brainstorm concept art if output does not reach players (sources: https://80.lv/articles/steam-has-clarified-its-rules-on-the-use-of-ai-in-video-games, https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/valve-has-significantly-rewritten-steams-rules-for-how-developers-much-disclose-ai-use, https://gamedeveloper.com/business/valve-tweaks-and-clarifies-ai-disclosure-rules-for-steam). 80.lv calls the change possibly "largely cosmetic" because Valve likely never enforced dev-only disclosure (source: https://80.lv/articles/steam-has-clarified-its-rules-on-the-use-of-ai-in-video-games). Gamingbible's author objects that concept art stages go undisclosed (source: https://www.gamingbible.com/news/platform/steam/steam-ai-changes-disclosure-rules-203740-20260120).
- Free-form text with no official tag leaves shoppers unable to search or filter; it is "not clear what happens" when a developer fails to disclose (source: https://stuff.co.za/2026/02/12/are-video-game-developers-using-ai-players-want-to-know-but-the-rules-are-patchy/). The fetched Steamworks page has no AI-specific enforcement or removal language, and says survey answers changed after approval require contacting Steam support (source: https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/gettingstarted/contentsurvey).
- The in-game overlay report that Valve announced in 2024 is for live-generated content that guardrails should have caught; it does not cover reporting undisclosed AI (sources: https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/steam-pages-will-now-disclose-which-games-use-ai-generated-content/, https://dashfight.com/news/steam-adds-an-option-to-report-ai-content-4901).
- Placement: the section sits at the bottom of the store page in the same format as mature content notes and is "remarkably easy to miss" (source: https://indiecator.org/2026/06/16/steam-next-fest-has-an-ai-problem-and-players-cant-filter-it-out/; single opinion blog).
- A claim that Valve changed the survey wording silently in May to June 2026 (artland3d, citing Wayback snapshots of 2026-05-13 and 2026-06-17) conflicts with contemporaneous coverage dating the "efficiency gains" wording to 2026-01-16 and later; treat it as unreliable (source: https://artland3d.com/steam-ai-disclosure-rules/, versus the three January sources above).

Named examples: AI used, not disclosed (at the time)

- The Alters (11 bit studios): launched 2025-06-13; players found ChatGPT-style text in an in-game logbook and AI-looking Brazilian Portuguese localization; 80.lv on 2025-06-30 said the Steam page had no AI disclaimer, which it called a violation of Steam's rules (source: https://80.lv/articles/the-alters-developer-gets-criticized-for-not-disclosing-ai-use). The studio's 2025-06-30 statement said AI assets were temporary placeholders, one shipped by accident, AI was used for last-minute translation of licensed movie subtitles (~0.3% of text), and it apologised for not telling players; it did not commit to a Steam disclosure (source: https://gameinformer.com/2025/06/30/11bit-studios-responds-to-the-alters-generative-ai-controversy). A June 2026 opinion piece says no disclosure has appeared on the page (source: https://indiecator.org/2026/06/16/steam-next-fest-has-an-ai-problem-and-players-cant-filter-it-out/; single source, unverified).
- Crimson Desert (Pearl Abyss): players spotted AI-looking 2D props about a day after launch; Pearl Abyss admitted on 2026-03-22 that placeholder assets made with "experimental AI generative tools" were "unintentionally included in the final release" and promised an audit; the Steam page "now" carries a disclosure, i.e. it was added after launch (source: https://engadget.com/gaming/crimson-desert-developer-apologizes-and-promises-to-replace-ai-generated-art-183716439.html). Players asked for refunds citing the late disclosure; Valve refused (ixbt, 2026-03-24, no Valve statement quoted) (source: https://ixbt.games/en/news/2026/03/24/valve-otkazalas-vozvrashhat-dengi-za-crimson-desert-igroki-nedovolny-naliciem-ii-assetov-v-igre.html). A search summary of a Notebookcheck article (403 on fetch) says the stated reason was the two-hour playtime limit: unverified (https://www.notebookcheck.net/Crimson-Desert-player-denied-Steam-refund-for-post-release-date-generative-AI-disclosure.1257901.0.html).
- Call of Duty: Black Ops 6 (Activision): launched October 2024; Steam page gained a disclosure reported 2025-02-25 reading "Our team uses generative AI tools to help develop some in-game assets", without saying which (source: https://decrypt.co/307729/call-of-duty-black-ops-6-generative-ai). This is both a late disclosure and a vague one.
- Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 (Sandfall): the Indie Game Awards rescinded two awards in December 2025 after Sandfall confirmed genai use, which it described as placeholder textures removed within days (sources: https://www.videogameschronicle.com/news/clair-obscur-expedition-33-game-of-the-year-award-pulled-after-admitting-to-generative-ai-use, headline only; https://stevivor.com/news/clair-obscur-loses-two-indie-game-awards-due-to-ai-usage/, search summary). When fetched on 2026-10-20 the Steam store page showed no AI disclosure section (source: https://store.steampowered.com/app/1903340/Clair_Obscur_Expedition_33/; single fetch via summariser). This is arguably compliant under the Jan 2026 rules because the textures did not ship. An indiecator claim that the game launched with a disclosure that was removed days later is single-source: unverified.

Named examples: retroactive and late disclosures, removals

- Haro's Wayback analysis: ~1% of pre-2024 games carry the flag and all of it is retroactive; 22% of significant-revenue AI games added the flag after release (example Crime Scene Cleaner, +20 months); these additions "cluster tightly" around Valve's January 2026 rewrite, which Haro reads as the signature of a compliance sweep (his inference; Valve made no statement); part of the 2026 rise is relabeling of older games (source: https://fragwyz.substack.com/p/three-years-of-ai-on-steam). The 22% is for significant-revenue games only; no full-census figure is given.
- An anecdote on the Steam forums: a user reported a game for non-disclosure and the developer added the disclosure retroactively; no game named (source: https://steamcommunity.com/discussions/forum/0/565912032657840371/).
- Totally Human notes some disclosures belong to old games updated later; example Stellaris, which predates the transformer paper (source: https://totallyhuman.io/blog/games-with-ai-disclosures-have-grossed-an-estimated-660m-on-steam).
- Removal of a disclosure: Jurassic World Evolution 3 (Frontier) replaced AI scientist portraits after backlash on 2025-06-25 and, per Hitmarker, the Steam page no longer shows the AI warning (source: https://hitmarker.net/news/frontier-announces-it-will-remove-ai-artwork-from-jurassic-world-evolution-3-following-player-backlash-1473986); Gamereactor reports the statement but not the disclosure removal (source: https://www.gamereactor.eu/jurassic-world-evolution-3-will-no-longer-use-generative-ai-after-fans-complained-1565003/). Treat the removal as single-source. Indiecator also says some games remove disclosures after replacing AI assets (single source, unverified). Haro's article found no dropped flags in its content, and did not look for them (source: https://fragwyz.substack.com/p/three-years-of-ai-on-steam).
- Messaging drift: a search summary of Eurogamer's Next Fest piece describes a developer whose wording moved from "AI created background assets" to "only used as reference"; original Eurogamer text not retrieved: unverified.

Vague or minimizing wording

- Haro's text analysis (138 successful and 400 flopped AI-flagged games): flops have shorter disclosures (median 13 words vs 22; 35% are one line of 10 words or fewer vs 13%); successful games use more minimizing language (59% vs 41%) and human-oversight reassurance (21% vs 12%), e.g. "reviewed and manually refined", "We do NOT use AI-generated art", and hedges like "Generative AI may have been used" (source: https://fragwyz.substack.com/p/three-years-of-ai-on-steam).
- Totally Human: among $1m+ earners most disclosures describe light, peripheral use with notes such as "no gameplay impact" and "under 1% of content" (source: https://totallyhuman.io/blog/games-with-ai-disclosures-have-grossed-an-estimated-660m-on-steam).
- GamingOnLinux (2025-10-21): wording ranges from specific to a vague "we may use it for background stuff" (source: https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2025/10/want-to-avoid-ai-gen-on-steam-this-browser-userscript-might-save-your-day/).

Valve forcing a disclosure or delisting

- No report was found of Valve delisting a game already on sale for undisclosed AI, and the conversation piece says Valve could pull titles hit by AI copyright claims but does not say it has (source: https://stuff.co.za/2026/02/12/are-video-game-developers-using-ai-players-want-to-know-but-the-rules-are-patchy/).
- Before the disclosure regime, in 2023, Valve rejected submissions containing AI assets over unclear training-data rights; this is pre-2024 history and seen only through search summaries of techcrunch and nme (https://techcrunch.com/2023/07/03/valve-responds-to-claims-it-has-banned-ai-generated-games-from-steam/): `search-summary`.
- A 2026 claim that Valve now blocks releases that skip AI metadata tagging came from one weak source (tech-insider.org) and has no corroboration: unverified.

### 3. The public debate and the state as of 2026-10-20

- Tim Sweeney, on X (reported by GamingOnLinux 2025-11-27), replying to an unnamed user who wanted Steam to drop "made with AI": "It makes no sense for game stores, where AI will be involved in nearly all future production"; he said the tag is relevant to art exhibits and licensing marketplaces; no Valve response in that article (source: https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2025/11/according-to-epic-ceo-tim-sweeney-game-stores-dont-need-an-ai-label-as-it-will-be-everywhere/). Techloy repeated it on 2025-12-02, adding Nexon CEO Junghun Lee saying it is "important to assume that every game company is using AI" (source: https://www.techloy.com/epic-ceo-tim-sweeney-says-steam-should-ditch-its-made-with-ai-labels/). The "shampoo brand" jab appears only in a search summary: unverified.
- Sweeney in a PC Gamer interview, relayed by VGC on 2026-06-25: "I think it's really irresponsible of Valve", the disclosure is an AI "Scarlet Letter", a "hater community" tries to kill games; no Valve response included; interview date not stated (source: https://videogameschronicle.com/news/epic-games-ceo-says-its-really-irresponsible-of-steam-to-make-studios-disclose-ai-use).
- Player side: players keep asking for a native filter; as of the June 2026 Next Fest coverage Steam offers none, and SteamDB's tag is the workaround (sources: https://indiecator.org/2026/06/16/steam-next-fest-has-an-ai-problem-and-players-cant-filter-it-out/, https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2025/02/steamdb-now-lets-you-filter-out-steam-games-with-ai-generation/). A resetera commenter predicts a filter would lead to "no dev disclosing AI use" (speculation) (source: https://www.resetera.com/threads/steam-next-fest-has-over-8-600-demos-and-almost-1700-of-them-have-ai-disclosures.1551832/).
- Commercial effect of the label: Haro finds AI-flagged games reach 100+ reviews at ~55% of the non-AI rate and hold about 10 to 27 percent of estimated sales against ~33% of launches (source: https://fragwyz.substack.com/p/three-years-of-ai-on-steam); a December 2025 "game oracle" analysis reportedly found about half the first-month reviews for disclosing games after controls and is correlational (reported by https://artland3d.com/steam-ai-disclosure-rules/; primary not retrieved: unverified). This is the incentive behind concealment and behind Sweeney's complaint.
- Player perception: an arXiv paper (Bazzaz and Cooper, 2026-08-12, 508,192 English Steam reviews) finds disclosing games get fewer recommendations and more negative sentiment than procedural-generation games, with players reading AI as low developer investment (source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11539).
- Valve signals: the only observed movement is the January 2026 narrowing; the disclosure itself stayed. Searches for September and October 2026 changes found nothing, and no Valve statement defending, changing or dropping the requirement was found. State as of 2026-10-20: requirement active, no native filter or tag found in coverage up to June 2026; absence of news proves nothing about changes; re-check the Steamworks Content Survey page before shipping.

### 4. Implications for the extension

Expected false negatives (game uses AI, signal absent)

- AI in dev tools and unshipped placeholder art is exempt by rule (sources in section 2).
- AI shipped but not disclosed, then fixed only after exposure: The Alters, Crimson Desert, Black Ops 6 (about a year late). A point-in-time scrape misses the window before the fix.
- Strategic omission: no incentive to disclose and a stigma ("Scarlet Letter") (Sweeney source in section 3; ResetEra #19 "only the ppl that are willing to disclose, in an environment with no incentive to disclose" is commenter opinion).
- Vague wording that a reader (or a classifier) does not recognise as AI.
- Every count above is a floor (VGC, Totally Human, techraptor all say this).

Expected false positives (flag shown, "uses AI" is misleading)

- Minor or peripheral use: the flag is binary and covers anything from one asset to live generation (source: https://fragwyz.substack.com/p/three-years-of-ai-on-steam).
- Marketing-only or store-page-only AI: the form covers marketing; the flag can mean no in-game AI (source: https://80.lv/articles/steam-has-clarified-its-rules-on-the-use-of-ai-in-video-games).
- Negated or reassuring text in the disclosure ("We do NOT use AI-generated art"); a keyword match on "AI" in the text is unsafe. Key off the section's presence, then show the text (Haro quotes above).
- Stale disclosures after assets were removed (jwe3 shows the page can be updated; whether most developers do it is unknown).
- Older games relabeled in a compliance sweep (Haro) and DLC, demos and software: SteamDB's count covers "games and software" (the conversation).
- SteamDB tag mismatches reported by a reader comment (some undeclared games tagged, some declared games not excluded) are unverified (https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2025/02/steamdb-now-lets-you-filter-out-steam-games-with-ai-generation/).

Complementary signals

- User reviews that mention AI: usable as a secondary hint; the arXiv study shows AI talk is common and negative, but wrongful accusations and "witch hunts" exist; use it only as a weak "community suspects" cue (sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11539, https://stuff.co.za/2026/02/12/are-video-game-developers-using-ai-players-want-to-know-but-the-rules-are-patchy/).
- SteamDB "AI Content Disclosed" tag: a convenience mirror of the same store-page disclosure and no independent signal (https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2025/02/steamdb-now-lets-you-filter-out-steam-games-with-ai-generation/). Historical snapshots (Wayback, as Haro used) could detect late and removed disclosures.
- Curator lists and Steam community user tags for AI: not researched or not found in this pass; no confirmation that such lists or tags exist or are maintained: gap.
- Prior art: "AI warning for Steam" (GitHub seeeeew/aiwarningforsteam) is an extension plus userscript that shows the disclosure in a popup on store pages and blurs or hides disclosing games on search pages (sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seeeeew/aiwarningforsteam/main/README.md, https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2025/10/want-to-avoid-ai-gen-on-steam-this-browser-userscript-might-save-your-day/).
- Design consequences: wording should be "discloses AI use" (never "uses" or "AI-free"); show the developer's own text; absence of a disclosure should render as neutral and never as clean; consider a severity hint (in-game art vs marketing vs live-generated) from the pre/live structure.

## Caveats and version notes

- Policy versions: Jan 2024 original form; Jan 2026 rewrite (form reported on 2026-01-16 by Game Developer, 2026-01-17 by VGC, 2026-01-19 by 80.lv); the 2024 form asked about AI more broadly (gamingbible). Counts before and after the rewrite measure slightly different things.
- Sources differ on denominators (all releases, games only, games and software, event lists) and on snapshot dates; do not chart them as one series.
- The Steam store API `appdetails` response for app 1903340 and for the sample app 5072580 showed no dedicated AI-disclosure field in a single summariser read (the sample's short description and pc requirements mention AI narration and omit the disclosure section); the disclosure appears to live in the store page HTML. This is one read through a summariser: unverified, check directly before relying on it. The sample page (https://store.steampowered.com/app/5072580/Courage_and_Faith_Into_the_Dark_Woods/) was read as opening "Generative AI is used in both pre-generated and live-generated content." with no release date announced; developer Local Fire Games.
- Several outlets (PC Gamer, TechRadar, Notebookcheck, Screenhub, inkl) returned 403 or boilerplate; their content is known only through headlines or search summaries; each such claim is tagged.
- A search result from piefed.keyboardvagabond.com contained an embedded instruction-like string; it was not acted on and that site is not used as a source.
- Sub-questions not fully answered: no Valve statement on counts or on Sweeney; no confirmed Valve delisting for non-disclosure; no verified curator lists or user-tag signals; no first-hand check of the Steamworks page history for post-January-2026 edits.
```

`docs/research/steam-ai-disclosure/rq4-prior-art.md`:

```md
# RQ4: What prior art and data sources already exist for flagging AI-using games on Steam?

Researched 2026-10-20. All counts are snapshots from that day or from the dated article cited. Most pages were read through a summarising fetch tool. Exact strings and numbers marked "unverified" need a re-check against the primary page before they go into code or copy.

## Answer in short

- Four browser/userscript tools do what this project plans, all keyed on the store-page "AI Generated Content Disclosure" heading: "AI warning for Steam" (seeeeew, MIT, the clear market leader, about 5.5k Firefox users and about 10k Chrome users), "AI Generated Content Filter for Steam" (SoBloxsy/Iren, Apache-2.0, tiny), "Steam AI Games Indicator" (Pierre-Demessence, MIT, userscripts with a seeded app ID list and capsule badges) and "Obvious Steam AI" (banner only, MPL-2.0, no users listed). Augmented Steam has no such feature; the request (issue 1913) has been open since 2024-04 with no maintainer decision.
- None of them uses a first-party data feed. All scrape the English heading text, either from the open app page or by fetching `/app/<id>` once per search/wishlist row and caching 7 to 30 days. The only breakages on record are localisation breakages (Russian in 2026-02, French in 2026-09) plus a new language (Malay in 2026-06).
- Bulk app-id sources are weak: SteamDB has the "AI Content Disclosed" tag (ID 1368160, 14,367 titles on 2026-09-23 per a secondary report) but its FAQ forbids scraping, dumps and republishing; aitransparencyindex.com lists about 26,041 disclosures with app IDs but states no API, export or license; the only reusable app-id file found is `appids.json` (MIT, about 26k IDs, seeded from SteamDB) in Pierre-Demessence's repo. No kaggle/huggingface dataset found.
- Steam curators exist (for example "Games That Use AI Generation", 1,559 followers; "No AI", 1,353 followers) but are manual, opinion-laden and not machine-readable; useful as a false-positive signal and give no seed.
- Gaps competitors leave: the modal blocks the whole page and has no options, no coverage of wishlist/home capsules in the leader, no scope distinction (marketing-only vs in-game vs live), no publisher allow-list, false positives from disclosures that say AI was not used or only for upscaling/translation.

## Findings

### 1. Existing browser extensions, userscripts and curators

#### 1.1 AI warning for Steam (seeeeew)

- Identity and links: GitHub repo https://github.com/seeeeew/aiwarningforsteam; Firefox add-on https://addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/ai-warning-for-steam/; Chrome Web Store ID `clegcobheppnnigaaeelfkeomjcngmnh`; the same `aiwarningforsteam.user.js` file is also the userscript, installable from the repo raw URL (source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seeeeew/aiwarningforsteam/main/README.md).
- License: MIT, copyright seeeeew 2025 (source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seeeeew/aiwarningforsteam/main/LICENSE; confirmed by GitHub API https://api.github.com/repos/seeeeew/aiwarningforsteam).
- Activity: repo created 2025-05-17, last push 2026-09-25, 182 stars, 1 fork, 10 open issues, 20 commits on main (source: https://api.github.com/repos/seeeeew/aiwarningforsteam and https://api.github.com/repos/seeeeew/aiwarningforsteam/commits?per_page=30). Firefox version history: 0.2.5 (2025-10-21), 1.0.0 (2025-11-30), 1.0.1 (2025-12-02), 1.0.2 (2026-02-25, fixed Russian detection after a Steam string change), 1.0.3 (2026-06-13, Malay), 1.1.0 (2026-06-19, search blur/hide), 1.1.2 (2026-09-25, fixed French detection) (source: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/ai-warning-for-steam/versions/).
- Install counts: Firefox 5,475 users, 5/5 from 29 reviews, v1.1.2 updated 2026-09-25 (source: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/ai-warning-for-steam/). Chrome: the Web Store page could not be fetched (consent redirect); the count comes from third-party trackers: "10K" and 4.2 from 21 ratings (source: https://extscope.org/extension/clegcobheppnnigaaeelfkeomjcngmnh) and "10K+", v1.1.0 (source: https://chromeboard.com/extension/ai-warning-for-steam-clegcobheppnnigaaeelfkeomjcngmnh). Chrome figures are unverified against the store itself, and the trackers disagree on the version.
- Manifest: manifest v3, version 1.1.2, `permissions: ["storage"]`, no `host_permissions`, one content script matched to `*://store.steampowered.com/app/*` and `*://store.steampowered.com/search*`, gecko `data_collection_permissions.required: ["none"]` (source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seeeeew/aiwarningforsteam/main/manifest.json).
- How it detects: on an app page it queries `.game_page_autocollapse > #game_area_content_descriptors > h2` and compares the heading text with a table of localised heading strings (about 33 languages); on a match it clones the sibling content into a modal overlay. On the search page it reads `row.dataset.dsAppid` for each result row, fetches `https://store.steampowered.com/app/<appid>?l=english` and tests the HTML for the literal `<h2>AI Generated Content Disclosure</h2>`. Results are cached per app (key `app-<appid>`) for 30 days when positive and 7 days when negative, and entries older than the last extension update are ignored. A `MutationObserver` on `#search_results` handles rows loaded later. The only outbound request is that per-app store page fetch (source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seeeeew/aiwarningforsteam/main/aiwarningforsteam.user.js, read through a summariser twice with consistent results; the cache and fetch lines were quoted back, the full file was not reproduced).
- Where it shows: modal on the app page; blur or hide (user choice, stored as `filtermode`) on search result rows, with a "Narrow by AI Generated Content Disclosure" block in the search sidebar (same script source). Because the manifest only matches `/app/*` and `/search*`, it does not touch the home page, wishlist, tag/browse pages or event pages (inference from the manifest matches). The Firefox build also runs on Firefox for Android (source: README above). Steam desktop client is not supported (GitHub issue 3, open, users report running it through Millennium and Extendium; source: https://api.github.com/repos/seeeeew/aiwarningforsteam/issues?state=all&per_page=30).
- Open issues relevant to us: 2 (very long disclosures overlap the watermark and push the close button off screen), 3 (Steam client), 4 (add an automated check for changed heading strings), 12 (whitelist for developers/publishers because AI upscaling disclosures trigger the warning) (same issues source).
- Press: GamingOnLinux 2025-10-21 https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2025/10/want-to-avoid-ai-gen-on-steam-this-browser-userscript-might-save-your-day, gHacks 2025-10-29, Outlook Respawn 2025-12-02, games.gg 2026-06-30, Shane the Gamer 2026-10-20 (sources: https://respawn.outlookindia.com/gaming/gaming-news/free-ai-warning-tool-flags-generative-content-on-steam-store, https://games.gg/news/steam-ai-disclosure-plugin-sweeney-valve/, https://www.shanethegamer.com/news/steam-next-fest-ai-games-filter/). The gHacks page itself returned 403; its existence is from a search result only.
- A GreasyFork or OpenUserJS listing for it was not found; the author distributes the userscript from GitHub raw only (README above). A search that claimed a GreasyFork install path is unverified.

#### 1.2 AI Generated Content Filter for Steam (SoBloxsy / Iren, iren.blue)

- Links: GitHub https://github.com/SoBloxsy/AI-Content-Hider-for-Steam; Firefox https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/ai-content-filter-for-steam/; Chrome ID `fgkeoeoibigdcdkfdckkpodhfhppgdlo` (source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SoBloxsy/AI-Content-Hider-for-Steam/main/README.md).
- License: GitHub API reports Apache-2.0 and the Firefox listing says Apache License 2.0; the README itself states no license (sources: https://api.github.com/repos/SoBloxsy/AI-Content-Hider-for-Steam, https://addons.mozilla.org/en-GB/firefox/addon/ai-content-filter-for-steam/).
- Activity and adoption: repo created 2025-12-25, last push 2026-08-22, 2 stars, 1 open issue (GitHub API above). Firefox: 80 users, 5/5 from 2 reviews, v3.4.1 updated 2026-08-22 (Firefox listing). Chrome: about 1K installs, 3.7 from 3 ratings, one 1-star review "does not work (Brave)" (third-party tracker, unverified: https://extscope.org/extension/fgkeoeoibigdcdkfdckkpodhfhppgdlo).
- Manifest: v3, version 3.4.1, `permissions: ["storage"]`, service worker background, popup action, content script on `*://store.steampowered.com/*` at `document_end` (source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SoBloxsy/AI-Content-Hider-for-Steam/main/manifest.json).
- Detection (from `content.js`, summarised once, unverified in detail): on `/app/` pages it looks for an `<h2>` containing the English text "AI Generated Content Disclosure" inside `#game_area_content_descriptors` and prepends a red warning banner to `#responsive_apppage_details_left_ctn`, showing the disclosure text; elsewhere (search, tag pages, capsules, wishlist) it fetches `https://store.steampowered.com/app/<id>/` and string-matches; checks start when an item is within 200px of the viewport; cache `slop_cache_<appId>` in `chrome.storage.local` with a 7-day TTL; modes `hide`, `highlight`, `text` (default `text`, label "[AI CONTENT USED]"); wishlist supported, with `hide` falling back to `highlight`; English only; the app-page "hide" branch is empty (source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SoBloxsy/AI-Content-Hider-for-Steam/main/content.js). The summary showed no `?l=english` parameter on the fetch; a non-English store language would likely break detection on fetched pages (inference, unverified).
- Contact for bugs is an email address in the README, no issue-driven workflow evident (README above).

#### 1.3 Steam AI Games Indicator (Pierre-Demessence), userscripts

- Repo https://github.com/Pierre-Demessence/SteamAIGamesIndicator: two scripts, `steamAIBanner.user.js` (banner at the top of an app page, shows the disclosure text) and `steamAIBadge.user.js` v2.1 ("Uses AI" badges on store tiles, a "Hide items with AI disclosure" option in the search "Narrow by preferences" filter) (source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pierre-Demessence/SteamAIGamesIndicator/main/README.md).
- License MIT; created 2025-12-04, last push 2026-09-20, 2 stars, 0 open issues (source: https://api.github.com/repos/Pierre-Demessence/SteamAIGamesIndicator). Commit log shows wishlist support (2025-12-06 and again 2026-09-19), a fetch cache (2026-06-22), the search filter (2026-09-20) and home-page capsule pills (2026-09-20) (source: https://api.github.com/repos/Pierre-Demessence/SteamAIGamesIndicator/commits?per_page=30).
- Install is from GitHub raw URLs; the README lists no GreasyFork or OpenUserJS link (README above). Targets Tampermonkey, Violentmonkey and Greasemonkey.
- Detection and data (from the script source, summarised once): the userscript fetches `appids.json` from `raw.githubusercontent.com` (cached 24 h) and badges listed IDs immediately; for IDs not on the list it fetches `https://store.steampowered.com/app/<id>/?l=english` and tests a case-insensitive pattern for "AI Generated Content Disclosure", one request at a time with a 1 s delay, caching positives 30 days and negatives 7 days (negatives only if the page contains `id="appHubAppName"`, to skip age gates, login walls and error pages). It treats the list as complete up to the highest known app ID and never fetches lower IDs that are not on the list. `@grant` is `GM_xmlhttpRequest`, `GM_getValue`, `GM_setValue`; `@connect` is `store.steampowered.com` and `raw.githubusercontent.com`; `@match` is `https://store.steampowered.com/*`. The script itself makes no SteamDB call (source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pierre-Demessence/SteamAIGamesIndicator/main/steamAIBadge.user.js).
- Selectors it covers (useful list of surfaces): `.CapsuleDecorators` (modern capsules), `.ds_flagged`, `.tab_item`, `.search_result_row`, wishlist rows (`[data-rfd-draggable-id^="WishlistItem-"]`), home/sale capsules via `[data-ds-appid]` variants (same source). It is the only tool found that covers wishlist and home capsules.
- The README says Steam began requiring the disclosure "in late 2024", which conflicts with the January 2024 start reported elsewhere (see https://respawn.outlookindia.com/gaming/gaming-news/free-ai-warning-tool-flags-generative-content-on-steam-store); treat the README as imprecise.

#### 1.4 Obvious Steam AI (GothicMess), Firefox only

- Adds a banner at the top of store pages for games that disclose AI; v1.0, last updated 2025-12-19, no users or reviews listed, license MPL-2.0, permission is access to `store.steampowered.com`, no source repository on the listing (source: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/obvious-steam-ai/).

#### 1.5 other tools seen only in search results (unverified)

- "AI Slop Filter for Steam": described by one search summary as a newer extension that scans description, tags, developer name and images for slop/asset-flip signs rather than the disclosure, Chromium first, Firefox in development. Not opened; URL from a search result summary, treat everything about it as unverified (https://helpfulinfoforyou.com/2026/07/steam-ai-filter-browse-and-hide-generative-ai-games/).
- An itch.io port of the "AI warning" idea was mentioned in a search result (https://piefed.nullspace.lol/post/68020); not opened, unverified.
- GreasyFork: a search restricted to GreasyFork, SleazyFork and OpenUserJS returned no script that flags AI disclosure (only unrelated "Steam AI Agent Chat" and a wishlist sidebar; source: https://greasyfork.org/en/scripts/by-site/steampowered.com). This negative comes from one search engine pass and is no exhaustive listing; treat as "none found".
- Chrome Web Store: two disclosure-specific extensions came up (AI warning for Steam, AI Generated Content Filter for Steam); the rest were unrelated Steam utilities (search result titles only: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/ai-warning-for-steam/clegcobheppnnigaaeelfkeomjcngmnh).

#### 1.6 Augmented Steam (IsThereAnyDeal)

- No AI-disclosure feature as of 2026-10-20. Two open feature requests: issue 1913 "Option to see warning about games with AI generated content" (opened 2024-04-25, about 10 comments, 12 thumbs-up) and issue 2362 "Allow us to filter games with generative AI content from the store" (opened 2026-08-13, 0 comments, label `augmentation`) (sources: https://api.github.com/search/issues?q=repo:IsThereAnyDeal/AugmentedSteam+AI+disclosure&per_page=20, https://api.github.com/repos/IsThereAnyDeal/AugmentedSteam/issues/2362).
- The only maintainer-side comments in 1913 are from a collaborator in April 2024: it is tricky because other content-descriptor sections look the same; the heading text is the only discriminator, and text matching may break when Steam localises it. No decision to implement is recorded. In 2025-08 a commenter proposed using Steam's internal app key 565 (labelled `aicontenttype`, values empty/1/2) instead of text. On 2025-10-27 seeeeew offered the MIT code for reuse but said they were too busy to contribute it. On 2026-06-22 and 2026-10-19 commenters said they dislike the standalone extension's full-page modal and search blurring and want a dismissible banner like the DRM one (source: https://api.github.com/repos/IsThereAnyDeal/AugmentedSteam/issues/1913/comments, plus the issue page https://github.com/IsThereAnyDeal/AugmentedSteam/issues/1913; the comment summary was read twice and agreed).
- Adjacent AI feature: VaporLens (LLM review summaries) was added in v4.5.0 enabled by default, drew complaints, and in v4.6.0 stayed on by default but collapsed after a GitHub poll (158 votes, 66% keep) (source: https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2026/01/augmented-steam-browser-plugin-added-ai-features-from-vaporlens/). This is a data point that AI-related defaults are contentious in this audience.
- Scale and licence: GPL-3.0, 1,785 stars, 127 forks, 360 open issues, default branch `develop`, last push 2026-10-16 (source: https://api.github.com/repos/IsThereAnyDeal/AugmentedSteam). Firefox: 64,156 users, 4.6/5 from 549 reviews, v5.0.0 updated 2026-10-02; required host access to `steampowered.com`, `store.steampowered.com`, `steamcommunity.com`; optional access to `steampowered.com`, `isthereanydeal.com`, `steamcommunity.com` (source: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/augmented-steam/). The Chrome store page was not fetched.
- Architecture (for reference): TypeScript + Svelte 4 + esbuild build (`scripts/build.mjs`), `webextension-polyfill`, `protobufjs`, `zod`, `idb`, `dompurify`; `src/js` has `Background`, `Content`, `Core`, `Options`, `Steam`; content code is organised by page class (`Page.ts`, `StorePage.ts`, `ReactPage.ts`, `LegacyPage.ts`, `CommunityPage.ts`) with per-page feature classes under `Features/Store/{App,Search,Wishlist,...}` and one file per feature (about 48 under `Store/App`, named `F<Feature>.ts` with optional `.svelte` views); a separate backend repo (`AugmentedSteam_Server`) is referenced by the README (sources: https://api.github.com/repos/IsThereAnyDeal/AugmentedSteam/contents/src/js/Content/Features/Store/App, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IsThereAnyDeal/AugmentedSteam/develop/package.json, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IsThereAnyDeal/AugmentedSteam/develop/README.md). The manifest was not retrieved (`develop/manifest.json` returned 404; presumably generated by the build, unverified). Splitting `ReactPage` from `LegacyPage` is itself evidence that Steam store pages are a mix of old server-rendered markup and newer react surfaces (inference).
- The extension is GPL-3.0; code cannot be copied into a permissively licensed project; seeeeew's MIT code and Pierre-Demessence's MIT scripts can.

#### 1.7 Steam curators

- "Games That Use AI Generation": https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45944619-Games-That-Use-AI-Generation/ , 1,559 followers, about 1,979 "Not Recommended" and 20 "Informational" reviews, covers 2026 releases that disclose AI; lists include "Possible Mistaken Use of AI Disclosure" (five games named), "2026 Releases That Have Removed The AI Disclosure From Their Page" and "...Removed The AI Content From Their Games"; most recent visible review 18 May (year not shown); detection is by reading disclosures, no stated verification process (same URL, page read once; counts internally inconsistent).
- "No AI": https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45186708-No-AI/ , 1,353 followers, "Informational" reviews, one list ("Discreet AI"); evidence cited per game includes store disclosures, developer statements, devlog videos and a third-party article; it also flags undisclosed use; entries from 2025-03-14 to at least 30 August; the page warns it contains adult-only titles; counts on the page are inconsistent.
- Other AI-themed curators from a search result list, details unverified: "AI Generated Slop" (curator/44890611), "NO AI #HumanArtists" (curator/45131686), "No AI games" (curator/45259214), "Does This Game Use GenAI?" (curator/45663731, labels "Gen AI used", "No gen AI used", "Unsure") (source: search results; example page https://store.steampowered.com/curator/44890611-AI-Generated-Slop/). A search summary also mentioned an "AI Check" curator group; it could not be located and is unverified. A Steam community group "GENAIORNAH" keeps a list from public statements and news (https://steamcommunity.com/groups/GENAIORNAH, from a search snippet only).
- A curator list would show up on store pages through Steam's own curator UI, and the extension's code plays no part; none exposes a documented bulk export (no documented export found; absence of evidence).

### 2. Bulk lists and datasets of AI-disclosed app IDs

#### 2.1 SteamDB

- Yes, there is a filter: the user tag "AI Content Disclosed", tag ID 1368160, page https://steamdb.info/tag/1368160 . Per the tag page text surfaced in a search result, SteamDB applies it automatically when the disclosure statement appears on the store page, and it covers disclosures about the product or its marketing; it does not tell in-game from marketing-only (source: search result snippet for https://steamdb.info/tag/1368160 ; the page itself returns 403 to automated fetch; the snippet is unverified against the page). To exclude in a SteamDB search, append `&tagid=-1368160` (source: https://www.destructoid.com/how-to-filter-out-generative-ai-games-with-steamdb/ , 2025-02-27).
- Size over time: more than 4,900 at launch on 2025-02-25 (https://videogameschronicle.com/news/steamdb-now-lets-players-filter-out-games-that-use-generative-ai); 12,284 on 2025-10-21 (https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2025/10/want-to-avoid-ai-gen-on-steam-this-browser-userscript-might-save-your-day); 14,367 cumulative as of a query on 2026-09-23, split 7,311 up to 2025 and 7,056 from 2026 releases (https://gameoverdrive.com.br/steamdb-filtrar-jogos-ia-generativa-steam/ , secondary).
- Access and licence: SteamDB has no public API, offers no data access or dumps, does not allow scraping or crawling, prohibits publishing its data in its entirety and prohibits using it to train AI models; it points people to Steam's own web APIs, SteamKit or store-page parsing instead (source: https://steamdb.info/faq/ , read twice with matching quotes; also paraphrased in a search result). Conclusion: do not scrape SteamDB to seed the list. Note that `appids.json` in Pierre-Demessence's repo is documented as "sourced from SteamDB's AI-related tag" (README above); reusing that file inherits this risk even though the repo is MIT (the MIT licence on the repo does not grant rights SteamDB never gave; the legal view is undecided and not established here).
- Data-quality note: a GamingOnLinux reader reported that some games with no visible AI declaration carry `aicontenttype 1` in SteamDB metadata, and that some declared games still appear when the tag is excluded (anecdotal, https://www.gamingonlinux.com/2025/02/steamdb-now-lets-you-filter-out-steam-games-with-ai-generation/).

#### 2.2 Steam itself (first-party signal)

- Steamworks has an internal app key reported as `common_aicontenttype` (value empty, 1 pre-generated, 2 live-generated), cited from a SteamDB search and a Steamworks announcement titled "AI Content on Steam" (https://store.steampowered.com/news/group/4145017/view/3862463747997849618). The commenter calls it key 565; the announcement page returned only navigation text to the fetch tool; the key number and values are unverified; a second independent mention of "aicontenttype" exists in the GamingOnLinux reader comment above (same reader link).
- Public store APIs: for the sample app 5072580, `store.steampowered.com/api/appdetails` returned `content_descriptors` with `ids: [5]` and notes text, and no AI field; the only AI mentions are in the free-text `short_description` and `pc_requirements` (source: https://store.steampowered.com/api/appdetails?appids=5072580&l=english , one fetch, summariser output). `IStoreBrowseService/GetItems/v1` with a small `data_request` returned `content_descriptorids: [5]` and no AI key (source: https://api.steampowered.com/IStoreBrowseService/GetItems/v1 , one probe with a limited `data_request`; other `data_request` flags were not tried; this is not proof that no field exists). The store HTML for the same app does carry the heading "AI Generated Content Disclosure" in English followed by an italic paragraph, and no age gate was shown (source: https://store.steampowered.com/app/5072580/Courage_and_Faith_Into_the_Dark_Woods/?l=english). The HTML section is the only confirmed first-party public signal. Details belong to research question 2 (data surface).

#### 2.3 AI Transparency Index (aitransparencyindex.com)

- An independent tracker, a "Scrapeer" project run by Intuitive Systems Novesia UG (haftungsbeschraenkt); the home page on 2026-10-20 showed about 26,041 Steam disclosures (development only 1,503; store/marketing only 3,701; content in the game 18,087; live AI during play 816) and 871 new this week; mature-rated records are excluded by default (source: https://aitransparencyindex.com/ , https://aitransparencyindex.com/methodology , https://aitransparencyindex.com/about). An earlier count of more than 17,250 was reported 2026-07-13 (https://www.pcguide.com/news/more-than-17000-games-on-steam-now-come-with-an-ai-disclosure-30-use-ai-for-two-or-more-reasons/).
- Method: monitors Steam store metadata, extracts the disclosure text and classifies it with an LLM (currently Mistral) plus deterministic rules for negations, translation-only mentions and marketing vs in-game; no human review; no accuracy figure published; confidence is the model's own estimate (methodology page above).
- Format: a "Changelog" page lists recent items with date, game name, an app ID inside the link path `/products/steam/<id>` and a truncated excerpt (source: https://aitransparencyindex.com/changelog ; all entries were dated 2026-10-20 at fetch time).
- Reuse: no API, CSV, bulk download or licence is described (methodology and about pages above). It serves as a reference taxonomy (scope categories) and a cross-check, and it is no bulk seed unless the operator grants permission (unverified whether they would).

#### 2.4 research and journalism datasets

- Totally Human Media (2025-07-13): 7,818 of about 114,126 games had a disclosure, based on Steam's API; roughly 60% were visual-asset generation (secondary: https://wnhub.io/news/stores-and-publishing/item-48292 ; the primary post was not retrieved). No app ID list found.
- "Three years of AI on Steam" (Substack, 2026): census of 53,597 games released 2023-07 to 2026-07, about 9,400 flagged, first-appearance dates from the Wayback machine; says revenue and disclosure text are available as CSV but does not say whether app IDs are included and gives no data link (https://fragwyz.substack.com/p/three-years-of-ai-on-steam). No licence stated.
- Mendeley Data "Replication Data for The AI Disclosure Penalty in Digital Games", DOI 10.17632/zd77888mxw.1, 2026-06-25, CC BY 4.0, games released 2024-2025 with matched controls; whether app IDs and the disclosure flag columns are present is not confirmed by the page capture (files list empty in the fetch) (https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/zd77888mxw/1). Static and partial in time; unsuitable as a live seed.
- GG Insights monthly Steam CSV (gginsights.io, via https://hn.svelte.dev/item/43158425): tags, genres, prices; no AI disclosure field; no licence stated and a commenter quoted redistribution limits; not useful.
- Kaggle and Hugging Face: none found for AI-disclosed app IDs, but only web searches were run; those sites' own search was not used. itch.io has a self-applied "No AI" tag (https://itch.io/games/tag-no-ai); that is a different store and a "not using AI" signal, and the fetched count of 415,211 looks implausibly high; it is unverified.
- IsThereAnyDeal: a search found no AI tag or filter on the site; unverified (absence of evidence).
- GitHub: the only app-id list found is `appids.json` (JSON array of app IDs as quoted strings, sorted ascending, 385,906 bytes, highest ID seen 5286390; at about 15 bytes per line that is on the order of 26,000 entries, an estimate only). It is refreshed by hand: commits "added list of appIds" 2025-12-04, "update list of appids" 2026-06-22, "update appids.json" 2026-09-19 (sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pierre-Demessence/SteamAIGamesIndicator/main/appids.json , https://api.github.com/repos/Pierre-Demessence/SteamAIGamesIndicator/contents , commits URL above). Update frequency is therefore roughly quarterly.

### 3. What these tools do well and poorly

#### 3.1 done well

- Low privilege: the leader asks for `storage` only, with no `host_permissions`; install prompts therefore say little scary (manifest above). Firefox listings for the two extensions say no data collection (AMO listings above). Third-party tracker scoring flagged "medium risk" only because of `storage` (https://extscope.org/extension/clegcobheppnnigaaeelfkeomjcngmnh).
- Fast fixes: seeeeew shipped a fix for Russian within the same day of the issue's date range (issue 1 opened 2026-02-25 and release 1.0.2 dated 2026-02-25) and for French (issue 13 opened 2026-09-24, release 1.1.2 on 2026-09-25) (issues + versions sources above). Userscript updates arrive immediately, store builds wait for review (Shane the Gamer article, above).
- Sane cache: positive 30 days, negative 7 days, invalidation on extension update (user.js source above); the badge userscript adds a 1 s request delay and an age-gate guard (`appHubAppName`) before caching a negative.
- Localisation: only the leader maps the heading in about 33 languages; the other two tools are English only or rely on `?l=english` fetches.
- Dual packaging: one source file serves as userscript and MV3 content script (leader), which matches the pairing planned here.

#### 3.2 done poorly or not at all

- Blocking modal and no options: the leader opens a full-page modal that covers unrelated Steam UI and has no settings for the app page; two Augmented Steam commenters call it heavy-handed and want a banner like the DRM warning; one reports the developer has ruled out customisation (issue 1913 comments above; the "ruled out" claim is second-hand and unverified). The same commenter claims the extension was not updated since July, which conflicts with the 2026-09-25 release (AMO + commits); that claim is wrong or refers to something else.
- False positives by construction: tools flag the presence of the section and say nothing about actual AI use. Cases on record: a disclosure used to say no AI was used (a commenter names Crime Scene Cleaner), upscaling-only disclosures (issue 12), translation-only disclosures (reviewer reports aggregated by a tracker, unverified: https://extscope.org/extension/clegcobheppnnigaaeelfkeomjcngmnh), marketing-only disclosures counted by SteamDB, and curator lists that keep a "possible mistaken use of disclosure" list. Steam's own disclosure also separates pre-generated from live-generated content (research questions 1 (policy) and 2 (data surface)); none of the four tools surfaces that split in the badge.
- False negatives: all tools flag only disclosed games; undisclosed use is invisible (Shane the Gamer article and tool READMEs). The "No AI" curator covers some undisclosed cases manually.
- Localisation breakage: detection is a string compare on a localised `<h2>`. Russian broke when Steam changed a translation (issue 1, 2026-02-25), French broke (issue 13, 2026-09-24), Malay was added by Steam in 2026-06 and had to be added (issue 5), and issue 4 proposes a periodic automated heading check (issues source above). That is three heading-related events in about 11 months for the best maintained tool. The fetch-based paths (all tools) always request `?l=english` (leader, badge) or default language (filter extension, unverified), which sidesteps part of this at the cost of an extra request.
- Surface coverage: leader covers app pages and `/search*` only; the filter extension covers all `store.steampowered.com` pages but only English; the userscript badge tool covers capsules, search, wishlist and home but is a userscript with a hand-curated ID list. None is reported to cover the Steam client; GitHub issue 3 shows users working around with Millennium/Extendium.
- Network cost: search blur/hide and wishlist badging require one store-page fetch per unseen app, throttled in different ways (viewport-based observer, or a serial queue with 1 s delay). No issue about rate limiting was found in the leader's tracker (issues source), but large result pages imply many requests (inference).
- Stale seed lists: the badge tool assumes IDs below its highest known ID and absent from `appids.json` do not use AI and never fetches them; a game that adds a disclosure later is missed until the file is refreshed by hand, on a roughly quarterly cadence (user.js and commit sources above).
- Markup churn is normal for Steam extensions: Augmented Steam's recent log shows selector updates for the product gallery (2026-09-21) and review summaries (2026-09-17) and 4.8.x hotfixes after Steam changes broke wishlists (sources: https://api.github.com/repos/IsThereAnyDeal/AugmentedSteam/commits?per_page=15 , https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IsThereAnyDeal/AugmentedSteam/develop/changelog.yml).
- Reviews: tracker-collected reviews of the leader mention false flags and one miss, and ask for a way to report false flags (unverified, aggregated by a third party). No tool has a user-report or per-game override.

#### 3.3 positioning notes (inference from the above)

- Unserved needs visible in public feedback: non-blocking banner or badge (instead of a modal), per-surface toggles, a publisher/app allow-list, a visible split of "in game", "marketing only", "dev only", "live", wishlist and home capsule coverage in the browser extension, and an automated canary for heading changes in each store language.
- Licensing for reuse: seeeeew MIT (code and the localised heading table), Pierre-Demessence MIT, SoBloxsy Apache-2.0 per GitHub API, Augmented Steam GPL-3.0 (do not copy), SteamDB data not reusable per its FAQ.

## Caveats and version notes

- Most numbers came from fetches summarised by a small model; GitHub API numbers (stars, dates, licences) and the manifest/user.js facts were each seen once or twice with consistent results. Re-verify before quoting externally.
- Chrome Web Store pages (consent redirect) and steamdb.info (403) could not be read directly. Chrome install counts are from extscope and chromeboard, which disagree on version (1.1.2 vs 1.1.0) and are unverified against the store.
- Counts of disclosed games differ by method and date: 4,900 (2025-02), 12,284 (2025-10), 14,367 (SteamDB cumulative, 2026-09-23), about 17,250 (aitransparencyindex, 2026-07) and about 26,041 (aitransparencyindex, 2026-10-20), 7,818 (Totally Human Media, 2025-07). The index and SteamDB may count different sets (the index counts per-product records including software and excludes mature records by default; SteamDB's reported 15,000 included "games and software" per one search summary, unverified).
- Policy change: Valve narrowed what must be disclosed in January 2026 (background coding tools no longer need disclosure); old and new disclosures may not mean the same thing (secondary, from search summaries; see research question 1 (policy)).
- The web search tool summaries occasionally contradicted fetched pages (for example a claim of a GreasyFork listing); where they conflicted the fetched page was used and the claim marked unverified.
- Sub-question not fully answered: GreasyFork, OpenUserJS and SleazyFork were checked with one site-restricted search only; the userscript managers' own search pages were not queried directly. Edge add-ons store was not checked.
- The existing file `docs/research/steam-ai-disclosure.md` is an empty template; this note is meant to feed the section on research question 4 (prior art).
```
